questions.q: The value of the integral $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{\sqrt{x(x^2+x+1)}}{(\sqrt{x+1})(\sqrt{x^4+x^2+1})} \, dx$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Let $I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{\sqrt{x(x^2 + x + 1)}}{\sqrt{x + 1}\,\sqrt{x^4 + x^2 + 1}}\, dx$.

Using the identity $x^4 + x^2 + 1 = (x^2 + x + 1)(x^2 - x + 1)$:
$I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{\sqrt{x}\,\sqrt{x^2 + x + 1}}{\sqrt{x + 1}\,\sqrt{(x^2 + x + 1)(x^2 - x + 1)}}\, dx$

Cancelling $\sqrt{x^2 + x + 1}$:
$I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{(x + 1)(x^2 - x + 1)}}\, dx$

Using $(x + 1)(x^2 - x + 1) = x^3 + 1$:
$I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x^3 + 1}}\, dx$

Substitution:
Let $t = x^{3/2}$, so $dt = \dfrac{3}{2}x^{1/2}\, dx \Rightarrow \sqrt{x}\, dx = \dfrac{2}{3}\, dt$.

Also, $t^2 = x^3$, so $x^3 + 1 = t^2 + 1$.

Changing limits:
$x = 0 \Rightarrow t = 0$
$x = 2 \Rightarrow t = 2^{3/2} = 2\sqrt{2}$

Therefore:
$I = \dfrac{2}{3}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\sqrt{2}} \dfrac{dt}{\sqrt{t^2 + 1}}$

Using $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dt}{\sqrt{t^2 + a^2}} = \log_e\left|t + \sqrt{t^2 + a^2}\right| + C$:
$I = \dfrac{2}{3}\left[\log_e\left(t + \sqrt{t^2 + 1}\right)\right]_{0}^{2\sqrt{2}}$

$I = \dfrac{2}{3}\left[\log_e\left(2\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{8 + 1}\right) - \log_e(1)\right]$

$I = \dfrac{2}{3}\log_e\left(2\sqrt{2} + 3\right)$

$I = \dfrac{2}{3}\log_e\left(3 + 2\sqrt{2}\right)$

Hence, the correct option is $(3)\ \dfrac{2}{3}\log_e\left(3 + 2\sqrt{2}\right)$.

questions.q: If $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4}\left(\cot\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\cot\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+1\right)dx = \alpha\log_e(\sqrt{3}-1)$, then $9\alpha^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.solution:
Given integral is $I = \displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4}\left(\cot\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\cot\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+1\right)dx$

Using the identity $\cot A \cot B + 1 = \dfrac{\cos(A-B)}{\sin A \sin B}$, the integrand simplifies to:

$f(x) = \dfrac{\cos\left(\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) - \left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right)}{\sin\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)}$

$f(x) = \dfrac{\cos\left(-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)}{\sin^2 x - \sin^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)}$

$f(x) = \dfrac{-1/2}{\sin^2 x - 3/4} = \dfrac{2}{3 - 4\sin^2 x}$

Dividing the numerator and the denominator by $\cos^2 x$:

$f(x) = \dfrac{2\sec^2 x}{3\sec^2 x - 4\tan^2 x} = \dfrac{2\sec^2 x}{3(1+\tan^2 x) - 4\tan^2 x} = \dfrac{2\sec^2 x}{3 - \tan^2 x}$

The integral becomes:

$I = \displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{2\sec^2 x}{3 - \tan^2 x} dx$

Substituting $\tan x = t \Rightarrow \sec^2 x dx = dt$.

When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, $t = 1$.

$I = \displaystyle\int_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{1} \dfrac{2}{3 - t^2} dt$

Using the standard integral $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{a^2 - x^2} dx = \dfrac{1}{2a}\ln\left|\dfrac{a+x}{a-x}\right|$:

$I = 2 \left[ \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} \ln\left|\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+t}{\sqrt{3}-t}\right| \right]_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{1}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \left( \ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{3}-1}\right) - \ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}{\sqrt{3}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}\right) \right)$

$I = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \left( \ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{3}-1}\right) - \ln\left(\dfrac{3+1}{3-1}\right) \right)$

$I = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \left( \ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{3}-1}\right) - \ln 2 \right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2(\sqrt{3}-1)}\right)$

Rationalizing the term inside the logarithm by multiplying the numerator and the denominator by $(\sqrt{3}-1)$:

$\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2(\sqrt{3}-1)} = \dfrac{(\sqrt{3}+1)(\sqrt{3}-1)}{2(\sqrt{3}-1)^2} = \dfrac{3-1}{2(\sqrt{3}-1)^2} = \dfrac{1}{(\sqrt{3}-1)^2} = (\sqrt{3}-1)^{-2}$

Thus,

$I = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \ln\left((\sqrt{3}-1)^{-2}\right) = -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \ln(\sqrt{3}-1)$

Comparing this with $I = \alpha\log_e(\sqrt{3}-1)$, we get:

$\alpha = -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$

Therefore, $9\alpha^2 = 9 \left(-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2 = 9 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = 12$.

Answer: $12$

questions.q: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & \alpha \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ be a singular matrix. Let $f(x) = \int\limits_0^x (t^2 + 2t + 3)\,dt$, $x \in [1, \alpha]$. If $M$ and $m$ are respectively the maximum and the minimum values of $f$ in $[1, \alpha]$, then $3(M - m)$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
Since $A$ is a singular matrix, $|A| = 0$.

$|A| = 1(-1 - \alpha) - 3(-2 - 0) - 1(2 - 0) = 0$

$-1 - \alpha + 6 - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha = 3$

The function is $f(x) = \int\limits_0^x (t^2 + 2t + 3)\,dt = \dfrac{x^3}{3} + x^2 + 3x$

Differentiating with respect to $x$, we get $f'(x) = x^2 + 2x + 3 = (x+1)^2 + 2 > 0$ for all $x$.

Thus, $f(x)$ is a strictly increasing function on the interval $[1, 3]$.

The maximum value $M$ occurs at $x = 3$:

$M = f(3) = \dfrac{3^3}{3} + 3^2 + 3(3) = 9 + 9 + 9 = 27$

The minimum value $m$ occurs at $x = 1$:

$m = f(1) = \dfrac{1^3}{3} + 1^2 + 3(1) = \dfrac{13}{3}$

We need to find $3(M - m)$:

$3(M - m) = 3\left(27 - \dfrac{13}{3}\right) = 81 - 13 = 68$

Answer: $68$

questions.q:
Let $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be such that $f(xy) = f(x)f(y)$, for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and $f(0) \neq 0$. Let $g: [1, \infty) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function such that
$x^2 g(x) = \int\limits_1^x (t^2 f(t) - tg(t))\,dt$.
Then $g(2)$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
Given $f(xy) = f(x)f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and $f(0) \neq 0$.

Substituting $y = 0$, we get $f(0) = f(x)f(0)$.

Since $f(0) \neq 0$, dividing by $f(0)$ gives $f(x) = 1$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

The given integral equation is:

$x^2 g(x) = \int\limits_1^x (t^2 f(t) - tg(t))\,dt$

Substituting $f(t) = 1$:

$x^2 g(x) = \int\limits_1^x (t^2 - tg(t))\,dt$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ using Leibniz's rule:

$2x g(x) + x^2 g'(x) = x^2 - xg(x)$

$x^2 g'(x) + 3xg(x) = x^2$

Dividing by $x$ (since $x \ge 1$):

$x g'(x) + 3g(x) = x$

$g'(x) + \dfrac{3}{x}g(x) = 1$

This is a linear differential equation. The integrating factor is:

$\text{IF} = e^{\int \dfrac{3}{x}\,dx} = e^{3\ln x} = x^3$

Multiplying the differential equation by $x^3$:

$x^3 g'(x) + 3x^2 g(x) = x^3$

$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^3 g(x)) = x^3$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$:

$x^3 g(x) = \dfrac{x^4}{4} + C$

From the integral equation, substituting $x = 1$ gives $1^2 g(1) = \int\limits_1^1 (t^2 - tg(t))\,dt = 0$, so $g(1) = 0$.

Substituting $x = 1$ and $g(1) = 0$ into the integrated equation:

$1^3(0) = \dfrac{1^4}{4} + C \Rightarrow C = -\dfrac{1}{4}$

Thus, the function $g(x)$ is given by:

$x^3 g(x) = \dfrac{x^4 - 1}{4}$

$g(x) = \dfrac{x^4 - 1}{4x^3}$

Substituting $x = 2$:

$g(2) = \dfrac{2^4 - 1}{4(2^3)} = \dfrac{16 - 1}{32} = \dfrac{15}{32}$

Answer: $\dfrac{15}{32}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The value of the integral $\int\limits_{-1}^{1} \left(\dfrac{x^3 + |x| + 1}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1}\right) dx$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_{-1}^{1} \left(\dfrac{x^3 + |x| + 1}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1}\right) dx$

We can split the integral into two parts:

$I = \int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{x^3}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1} dx + \int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{|x| + 1}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1} dx$

The first integrand $f(x) = \dfrac{x^3}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1}$ is an odd function since $f(-x) = -f(x)$. Therefore, its integral over the symmetric interval $[-1, 1]$ is zero.

The second integrand $g(x) = \dfrac{|x| + 1}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1}$ is an even function since $g(-x) = g(x)$. Therefore, its integral over $[-1, 1]$ is twice the integral over $[0, 1]$.

$I = 0 + 2 \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{x + 1}{x^2 + 2x + 1} dx$

$I = 2 \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{x + 1}{(x + 1)^2} dx$

$I = 2 \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{x + 1} dx$

$I = 2 [\log_e(x + 1)]_{0}^{1}$

$I = 2(\log_e 2 - \log_e 1) = 2\log_e 2$

Answer: $2\log_e 2$
questions.question: The value of the integral $\int\limits_{-1}^{1} \left(\dfrac{x^3 + |x| + 1}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1}\right) dx$ is equal to :
questions.explanation:
Let $I = \int_{-1}^{1} \left(\dfrac{x^3 + |x| + 1}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1}\right) dx$

$I = \int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{x^3}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1} dx + \int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{|x| + 1}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1} dx$

The first integrand $f(x) = \dfrac{x^3}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1}$ is an odd function since $f(-x) = -f(x)$. Therefore, its integral over the symmetric interval $[-1, 1]$ is zero.

The second integrand $g(x) = \dfrac{|x| + 1}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1}$ is an even function since $g(-x) = g(x)$. Therefore, its integral over $[-1, 1]$ is twice the integral over $[0, 1]$.

$I = 0 + 2 \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{x + 1}{x^2 + 2x + 1} dx$

$I = 2 \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{x + 1}{(x + 1)^2} dx$

$I = 2 \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{x + 1} dx$

$I = 2 [\log_e(x + 1)]_{0}^{1}$

$I = 2(\log_e 2 - \log_e 1) = 2\log_e 2$

Answer: $2\log_e 2$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The value of the integral $\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\left(\dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{\sin x}}\right)dx$ is:
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{\sin x}} dx$

Using the definite integral property $\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) dx = \int_{0}^{a} (f(x) + f(-x)) dx$, we get:

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \left( \dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{\sin x}} + \dfrac{32\cos^4(-x)}{1 + e^{\sin(-x)}} \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \left( \dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{\sin x}} + \dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{-\sin x}} \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \left( \dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{\sin x}} + \dfrac{32\cos^4 x \cdot e^{\sin x}}{e^{\sin x} + 1} \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} 32\cos^4 x \left( \dfrac{1 + e^{\sin x}}{1 + e^{\sin x}} \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} 32\cos^4 x dx$

Using the trigonometric identity $\cos^2 x = \dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}$, we can write:

$\cos^4 x = \left( \dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2} \right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} (1 + 2\cos 2x + \cos^2 2x)$

$\cos^4 x = \dfrac{1}{4} \left( 1 + 2\cos 2x + \dfrac{1 + \cos 4x}{2} \right) = \dfrac{3}{8} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x + \dfrac{1}{8}\cos 4x$

Substituting this back into the integral:

$I = 32 \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \left( \dfrac{3}{8} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x + \dfrac{1}{8}\cos 4x \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} (12 + 16\cos 2x + 4\cos 4x) dx$

Integrating term by term:

$I = \left[ 12x + 8\sin 2x + \sin 4x \right]_{0}^{\pi/4}$

$I = \left( 12\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) + 8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \sin(\pi) \right) - (0 + 0 + 0)$

$I = 3\pi + 8(1) + 0 = 3\pi + 8$

Answer: $3\pi + 8$

Using the definite integral property $\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) dx = \int_{0}^{a} (f(x) + f(-x)) dx$, we get:

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \left( \dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{\sin x}} + \dfrac{32\cos^4(-x)}{1 + e^{\sin(-x)}} \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \left( \dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{\sin x}} + \dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{-\sin x}} \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \left( \dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{\sin x}} + \dfrac{32\cos^4 x \cdot e^{\sin x}}{e^{\sin x} + 1} \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} 32\cos^4 x \left( \dfrac{1 + e^{\sin x}}{1 + e^{\sin x}} \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} 32\cos^4 x dx$

Using the trigonometric identity $\cos^2 x = \dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}$, we can write:

$\cos^4 x = \left( \dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2} \right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} (1 + 2\cos 2x + \cos^2 2x)$

$\cos^4 x = \dfrac{1}{4} \left( 1 + 2\cos 2x + \dfrac{1 + \cos 4x}{2} \right) = \dfrac{3}{8} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x + \dfrac{1}{8}\cos 4x$

Substituting this back into the integral:

$I = 32 \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \left( \dfrac{3}{8} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x + \dfrac{1}{8}\cos 4x \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} (12 + 16\cos 2x + 4\cos 4x) dx$

Integrating term by term:

$I = \left[ 12x + 8\sin 2x + \sin 4x \right]_{0}^{\pi/4}$

$I = \left( 12\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) + 8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \sin(\pi) \right) - (0 + 0 + 0)$

$I = 3\pi + 8(1) + 0 = 3\pi + 8$

Answer: $3\pi + 8$

questions.q: Let $(2^{1-a} + 2^{1+a})$, $f(a)$, $(3^a + 3^{-a})$ be in A.P. and $\alpha$ be the minimum value of $f(a)$. Then the value of the integral $\int_{\log_e(\alpha-1)}^{\log_e(\alpha)} \dfrac{dx}{(e^{2x} - e^{-2x})}$ is :
questions.solution:
Since $(2^{1-a} + 2^{1+a})$, $f(a)$, and $(3^a + 3^{-a})$ are in A.P., we have:

$2f(a) = 2^{1-a} + 2^{1+a} + 3^a + 3^{-a}$

$f(a) = (2^{-a} + 2^a) + \dfrac{1}{2}(3^a + 3^{-a})$

Using the AM-GM inequality, $x + \dfrac{1}{x} \ge 2$ for $x > 0$.

$2^a + 2^{-a} \ge 2$ and $3^a + 3^{-a} \ge 2$.

The minimum value of $f(a)$ occurs when $a = 0$.

$\alpha = f(0) = (2^0 + 2^0) + \dfrac{1}{2}(3^0 + 3^0) = 2 + 1 = 3$.

Now, we evaluate the integral:

$I = \int_{\log_e 2}^{\log_e 3} \dfrac{dx}{e^{2x} - e^{-2x}} = \int_{\log_e 2}^{\log_e 3} \dfrac{e^{2x}}{e^{4x} - 1} dx$

Let $e^{2x} = t \Rightarrow 2e^{2x} dx = dt$.

When $x = \log_e 2$, $t = e^{2\log_e 2} = 4$.

When $x = \log_e 3$, $t = e^{2\log_e 3} = 9$.

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{4}^{9} \dfrac{dt}{t^2 - 1}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \left[ \dfrac{1}{2} \log_e \left| \dfrac{t-1}{t+1} \right| \right]_{4}^{9}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{4} \left( \log_e \dfrac{8}{10} - \log_e \dfrac{3}{5} \right)$

$I = \dfrac{1}{4} \left( \log_e \dfrac{4}{5} - \log_e \dfrac{3}{5} \right) = \dfrac{1}{4} \log_e \left( \dfrac{4/5}{3/5} \right) = \dfrac{1}{4} \log_e \left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right)$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{4} \log_e\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)$

questions.q: Let $f: [1, \infty) \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ be a differentiable function defined as $f(x) = \int_1^x f(t)\,dt + (1-x)(\log_e x - 1) + e$. Then the value of $f(f(1))$ is :
questions.solution:
Given $f(x) = \int_1^x f(t)\,dt + (1-x)(\log_e x - 1) + e$

Substituting $x = 1$ in the given equation:

$f(1) = \int_1^1 f(t)\,dt + (1-1)(\log_e 1 - 1) + e$

$f(1) = 0 + 0 + e = e$

Differentiating the given equation with respect to $x$ using the Leibniz rule:

$f'(x) = f(x) + \dfrac{d}{dx}[(1-x)(\log_e x - 1)]$

$f'(x) = f(x) + (-1)(\log_e x - 1) + (1-x)\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)$

$f'(x) = f(x) - \log_e x + 1 + \dfrac{1}{x} - 1$

$f'(x) - f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x} - \log_e x$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$, where $P = -1$ and $Q = \dfrac{1}{x} - \log_e x$.

Integrating Factor (IF) $= e^{\int -1 \,dx} = e^{-x}$

Multiplying the differential equation by the IF:

$e^{-x} f'(x) - e^{-x} f(x) = e^{-x} \left(\dfrac{1}{x} - \log_e x\right)$

$\dfrac{d}{dx}[e^{-x} f(x)] = e^{-x} \dfrac{1}{x} - e^{-x} \log_e x$

Notice that $\dfrac{d}{dx}[e^{-x} \log_e x] = -e^{-x} \log_e x + e^{-x} \dfrac{1}{x}$.

Thus, $\dfrac{d}{dx}[e^{-x} f(x)] = \dfrac{d}{dx}[e^{-x} \log_e x]$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$:

$e^{-x} f(x) = e^{-x} \log_e x + C$

$f(x) = \log_e x + C e^x$

Using the initial condition $f(1) = e$:

$e = \log_e 1 + C e^1$

$e = 0 + C e \Rightarrow C = 1$

Therefore, the function is $f(x) = \log_e x + e^x$.

We need to find $f(f(1))$:

Since $f(1) = e$, we evaluate $f(e)$:

$f(e) = \log_e e + e^e = 1 + e^e$

Answer: $(1 + e^e)$

questions.q: The value of the integral $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty \dfrac{\log_e(x)}{x^2 + 4}\,dx$ is:
questions.solution:
Let $I = \displaystyle\int_0^\infty \dfrac{\log_e(x)}{x^2 + 4}\,dx$

Substitute $x = 2 \tan \theta$, which gives $dx = 2 \sec^2 \theta \,d\theta$.

The limits of integration change from $x = 0 \to \theta = 0$ to $x \to \infty \to \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

$I = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\log_e(2 \tan \theta)}{4 \tan^2 \theta + 4} (2 \sec^2 \theta) \,d\theta$

$I = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\log_e(2 \tan \theta)}{4 \sec^2 \theta} (2 \sec^2 \theta) \,d\theta$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log_e(2 \tan \theta) \,d\theta$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} (\log_e 2 + \log_e(\tan \theta)) \,d\theta$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \log_e 2 \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} 1 \,d\theta + \dfrac{1}{2} \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log_e(\tan \theta) \,d\theta$

Let $I_1 = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log_e(\tan \theta) \,d\theta$

Using the property $\displaystyle\int_0^a f(x)\,dx = \displaystyle\int_0^a f(a-x)\,dx$, we get:

$I_1 = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log_e\left(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)\right) \,d\theta = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log_e(\cot \theta) \,d\theta$

$I_1 = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log_e\left(\dfrac{1}{\tan \theta}\right) \,d\theta = -\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log_e(\tan \theta) \,d\theta = -I_1$

$2I_1 = 0 \Rightarrow I_1 = 0$

Substituting $I_1 = 0$ back into the equation for $I$:

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \log_e 2 \left[\theta\right]_0^{\pi/2} + 0$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \log_e 2 \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi \log_e 2}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi\log_e(2)}{4}$

questions.q: The value of the integral $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \left(\dfrac{4 - \csc^2 x}{\cos^4 x}\right) dx$ is:
questions.solution:
The given integral is $I = \displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \left(\dfrac{4 - \csc^2 x}{\cos^4 x}\right) dx$.

We can rewrite the integrand in terms of $\tan x and \sec x$. Using the identity $\csc^2 x = 1 + \cot^2 x = 1 + \dfrac{1}{\tan^2 x}$, we get:

$I = \displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \left(4 - 1 - \dfrac{1}{\tan^2 x}\right) \sec^4 x \, dx$

$I = \displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \left(3 - \dfrac{1}{\tan^2 x}\right) (1 + \tan^2 x) \sec^2 x \, dx$

Substitute $t = \tan x$, which gives $dt = \sec^2 x \, dx$.

The limits of integration change as follows:
When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.
When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$, $t = \sqrt{3}$.

The integral becomes:

$I = \displaystyle\int_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}} \left(3 - \dfrac{1}{t^2}\right) (1 + t^2) dt$

Expanding the integrand, we get:

$I = \displaystyle\int_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}} \left(3 + 3t^2 - \dfrac{1}{t^2} - 1\right) dt$

$I = \displaystyle\int_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}} \left(3t^2 + 2 - t^{-2}\right) dt$

Integrating with respect to $t$:

$I = \left[ t^3 + 2t + \dfrac{1}{t} \right]_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}}$

Substitute the upper limit $t = \sqrt{3}$:

$\left( \sqrt{3} \right)^3 + 2\sqrt{3} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = 3\sqrt{3} + 2\sqrt{3} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} = \dfrac{16\sqrt{3}}{3} = \dfrac{48}{3\sqrt{3}}$

Substitute the lower limit $t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$:

$\left( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right)^3 + 2\left( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right) + \sqrt{3} = \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}} + \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} + \sqrt{3} = \dfrac{1 + 6 + 9}{3\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{16}{3\sqrt{3}}$

Subtracting the lower limit value from the upper limit value:

$I = \dfrac{48}{3\sqrt{3}} - \dfrac{16}{3\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{32}{3\sqrt{3}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{32}{3\sqrt{3}}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The integral $\int_{0}^{1}\cot^{-1}(1+x+x^2)dx$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
$I = \int_{0}^{1}\cot^{-1}(1+x+x^2)dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{1}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{1+x+x^2}\right)dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{1}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{(x+1)-x}{1+(x+1)x}\right)dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{1}(\tan^{-1}(x+1)-\tan^{-1}x)dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{1}\tan^{-1}(x+1)dx - \int_{0}^{1}\tan^{-1}x dx$

Substituting $x+1 = t$ in the first integral:

$I = \int_{1}^{2}\tan^{-1}x dx - \int_{0}^{1}\tan^{-1}x dx$

Using integration by parts, $\int \tan^{-1}x dx = x\tan^{-1}x - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e(1+x^2)$

$I = \left[x\tan^{-1}x - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e(1+x^2)\right]_{1}^{2} - \left[x\tan^{-1}x - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e(1+x^2)\right]_{0}^{1}$

$I = \left(2\tan^{-1}2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 5 - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 2\right)\right) - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 2 - 0\right)$

$I = 2\tan^{-1}2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 5 - \dfrac{\pi}{2} + \log_e 2$

$I = 2\tan^{-1}2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 5 + \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 4 - \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$I = 2\tan^{-1}2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right) - \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

Answer: $2\tan^{-1}2-\dfrac{1}{2}\log_e\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right)-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$
questions.question: The integral $\int_{0}^{1}\cot^{-1}(1+x+x^2)dx$ is equal to:

$I = \int_{0}^{1}(\tan^{-1}(x+1)-\tan^{-1}x)dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{1}\tan^{-1}(x+1)dx - \int_{0}^{1}\tan^{-1}x dx$

Substituting $x+1 = t$ in the first integral:

$I = \int_{1}^{2}\tan^{-1}x dx - \int_{0}^{1}\tan^{-1}x dx$

Using integration by parts, $\int \tan^{-1}x dx = x\tan^{-1}x - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e(1+x^2)$

$I = \left[x\tan^{-1}x - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e(1+x^2)\right]_{1}^{2} - \left[x\tan^{-1}x - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e(1+x^2)\right]_{0}^{1}$

$I = \left(2\tan^{-1}2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 5 - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 2\right)\right) - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 2 - 0\right)$

$I = 2\tan^{-1}2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 5 - \dfrac{\pi}{2} + \log_e 2$

$I = 2\tan^{-1}2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 5 + \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 4 - \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$I = 2\tan^{-1}2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right) - \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

Answer: $2\tan^{-1}2-\dfrac{1}{2}\log_e\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right)-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

questions.q: Let $f$ be a twice differentiable function such that $f(x)=\int_{0}^{x}\tan(t-x)dt-\int_{0}^{x}f(t)\tan t\,dt$, $x \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. Then $f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+12f'\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ is equal to ______
questions.solution:
Given the function:

$f(x) = \int_{0}^{x} \tan(t-x) dt - \int_{0}^{x} f(t) \tan t \, dt$

First, we simplify the first integral. Let $u = x - t$, then $du = -dt$. When $t = 0$, $u = x$; when $t = x$, $u = 0$.

$\int_{0}^{x} \tan(t-x) dt = \int_{x}^{0} \tan(-u) (-du) = \int_{x}^{0} \tan u \, du = -\int_{0}^{x} \tan u \, du = -[\ln(\sec u)]_{0}^{x} = -\ln(\sec x) = \ln(\cos x)$

So, the equation becomes:

$f(x) = \ln(\cos x) - \int_{0}^{x} f(t) \tan t \, dt$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ using the Leibniz rule:

$f'(x) = \dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x} - f(x) \tan x$

$f'(x) + f(x) \tan x = -\tan x$

This is a linear first-order differential equation. The integrating factor (IF) is:

$\text{IF} = e^{\int \tan x \, dx} = e^{\ln(\sec x)} = \sec x$

Multiplying the differential equation by $\sec x$:

$f'(x) \sec x + f(x) \sec x \tan x = -\sec x \tan x$

$\dfrac{d}{dx} (f(x) \sec x) = -\sec x \tan x$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$:

$f(x) \sec x = -\sec x + C$

To find $C$, we use the initial condition. From $f(x) = \ln(\cos x) - \int_{0}^{x} f(t) \tan t \, dt$, substituting $x = 0$ gives $f(0) = \ln(1) - 0 = 0$.

$0 \cdot \sec 0 = -\sec 0 + C \Rightarrow 0 = -1 + C \Rightarrow C = 1$

Thus, $f(x) \sec x = 1 - \sec x$

$f(x) = \cos x - 1$

Now, we find the required derivatives:

$f'(x) = -\sin x$

$f''(x) = -\cos x$

Evaluating these at the given points:

$f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) - 1 = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 1$

$f'\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

Finally, substituting these values into the required expression:

$f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) + 12f'\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) + f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 12\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 1\right)$

$= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 6 + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 1 = 5$

Answer: $5$

questions.q: Let $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} (|\sin x| + [x \sin x])\,dx = 2(3 - \cos 2) + \beta$, where $[\cdot]$ is the greatest integer function. Then $\beta \sin\left(\dfrac{\beta}{2}\right)$ equals:
questions.solution:
Let $I = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} \left(|\sin x| + [x \sin x]\right) dx = I_1 + I_2$, where
$I_1 = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} |\sin x|\, dx$ and $I_2 = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} [x \sin x]\, dx$.

Evaluating $I_1$:
Since $|\sin x|$ is even, $I_1 = 2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} |\sin x|\, dx$.
For $x \in [0, 2]$, $2 < \pi$, so $\sin x \geq 0$ and $|\sin x| = \sin x$.
$I_1 = 2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \sin x\, dx = 2\left[-\cos x\right]_0^2 = 2(1 - \cos 2) = 2 - 2\cos 2$

Evaluating $I_2$:
Let $g(x) = x\sin x$. Then $g(-x) = (-x)\sin(-x) = x\sin x = g(x)$, so $g(x)$ is even, and hence $[x\sin x]$ is also even.
$I_2 = 2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} [x\sin x]\, dx$

Behaviour of $y = x\sin x$ on $[0, 2]$:
At $x = 0$, $y = 0$. At $x = 2$, $y = 2\sin 2 \approx 1.818$.
$y' = \sin x + x\cos x > 0$ on $[0, 2]$, so $y$ is strictly increasing on this interval.

Therefore, $x\sin x$ takes each value in $[0, 1.818]$ exactly once, and crosses $1$ at some unique $\alpha \in (0, 2)$ with $\alpha\sin\alpha = 1$.

For $x \in [0, \alpha)$: $0 \leq x\sin x < 1 \Rightarrow [x\sin x] = 0$
For $x \in [\alpha, 2]$: $1 \leq x\sin x < 2 \Rightarrow [x\sin x] = 1$

$I_2 = 2\left(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\alpha} 0\, dx + \displaystyle\int_{\alpha}^{2} 1\, dx\right) = 2(2 - \alpha) = 4 - 2\alpha$

Combining:
$I = I_1 + I_2 = (2 - 2\cos 2) + (4 - 2\alpha) = 6 - 2\cos 2 - 2\alpha$

Given $I = 2(3 - \cos 2) + \beta = 6 - 2\cos 2 + \beta$, so:
$6 - 2\cos 2 - 2\alpha = 6 - 2\cos 2 + \beta \Rightarrow \beta = -2\alpha$

Now:
$\beta \sin\left(\dfrac{\beta}{2}\right) = -2\alpha \sin\left(\dfrac{-2\alpha}{2}\right) = -2\alpha \sin(-\alpha) = 2\alpha\sin\alpha$

Since $\alpha\sin\alpha = 1$:
$\beta \sin\left(\dfrac{\beta}{2}\right) = 2 \cdot 1 = 2$

Hence, the correct option is $(2)\ 2$.

questions.q: The value of $\int_0^{20\pi} (\sin^4 x + \cos^4 x) \, dx$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_0^{20\pi} (\sin^4 x + \cos^4 x) \, dx$

Using the algebraic identity $a^2 + b^2 = (a+b)^2 - 2ab$, the integrand can be simplified:

$\sin^4 x + \cos^4 x = (\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x)^2 - 2\sin^2 x \cos^2 x$

Since $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$ and $2\sin x \cos x = \sin 2x$:

$\sin^4 x + \cos^4 x = 1 - \dfrac{1}{2} (2\sin x \cos x)^2 = 1 - \dfrac{1}{2} \sin^2 2x$

Using the half-angle formula $\sin^2 \theta = \dfrac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{2}$:

$\sin^4 x + \cos^4 x = 1 - \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{1 - \cos 4x}{2} \right) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} \cos 4x = \dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} \cos 4x$

Substituting this back into the integral:

$I = \int_0^{20\pi} \left( \dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} \cos 4x \right) \, dx$

$I = \left[ \dfrac{3}{4} x + \dfrac{1}{16} \sin 4x \right]_0^{20\pi}$

Evaluating the limits:

$I = \left( \dfrac{3}{4} (20\pi) + \dfrac{1}{16} \sin(80\pi) \right) - (0 + 0)$

Since $\sin(80\pi) = 0$:

$I = 15\pi$

Answer: $15\pi$

questions.q: Let $[\cdot]$ denote the greatest integer function. Then the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^3 \left(\dfrac{e^x + e^{-x}}{[x]!}\right) dx$ is :
questions.solution:
The given integral can be split at integer values of $x$ because of the greatest integer function $[x]$.

$\displaystyle I = \int_0^3 \left(\dfrac{e^x + e^{-x}}{[x]!}\right) dx$

$\displaystyle I = \int_0^1 \dfrac{e^x + e^{-x}}{0!} dx + \int_1^2 \dfrac{e^x + e^{-x}}{1!} dx + \int_2^3 \dfrac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2!} dx$

Since $0! = 1$, $1! = 1$, and $2! = 2$, we get:

$\displaystyle I = \int_0^2 (e^x + e^{-x}) dx + \dfrac{1}{2} \int_2^3 (e^x + e^{-x}) dx$

Integrating the terms:

$\displaystyle I = \left[ e^x - e^{-x} \right]_0^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} \left[ e^x - e^{-x} \right]_2^3$

$\displaystyle I = (e^2 - e^{-2} - (1 - 1)) + \dfrac{1}{2} (e^3 - e^{-3} - (e^2 - e^{-2}))$

$\displaystyle I = e^2 - e^{-2} + \dfrac{1}{2} e^3 - \dfrac{1}{2} e^{-3} - \dfrac{1}{2} e^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} e^{-2}$

$\displaystyle I = \dfrac{1}{2} e^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} e^3 - \dfrac{1}{2} e^{-2} - \dfrac{1}{2} e^{-3}$

$\displaystyle I = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( e^2 + e^3 - \dfrac{1}{e^2} - \dfrac{1}{e^3} \right)$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}\left(e^2 + e^3 - \dfrac{1}{e^2} - \dfrac{1}{e^3}\right)$

questions.q: If $\alpha = \displaystyle\int_0^{2\sqrt{3}} \log_2(x^2 + 4)\,dx + \displaystyle\int_2^4 \sqrt{2^x - 4}\,dx$, then $\alpha^2$ is equal to _______.
questions.solution:
Let $f(x) = \log_2(x^2 + 4)$ for $x \ge 0$.

To find the inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$, we set $y = \log_2(x^2 + 4)$ and solve for $x$:

$2^y = x^2 + 4$

$x^2 = 2^y - 4$

$x = \sqrt{2^y - 4}$

Thus, $f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{2^x - 4}$.

The given expression is $\alpha = \displaystyle\int_0^{2\sqrt{3}} f(x)\,dx + \displaystyle\int_2^4 f^{-1}(x)\,dx$.

We observe the limits of the first integral and evaluate the function at these points:

$f(0) = \log_2(0 + 4) = 2$

$f(2\sqrt{3}) = \log_2((2\sqrt{3})^2 + 4) = \log_2(12 + 4) = \log_2(16) = 4$

These exactly match the limits of the second integral. Using the standard property of definite integrals for inverse functions:

$\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx + \displaystyle\int_{f(a)}^{f(b)} f^{-1}(x)\,dx = b f(b) - a f(a)$

Substituting $a = 0$ and $b = 2\sqrt{3}$:

$\alpha = 2\sqrt{3} \cdot f(2\sqrt{3}) - 0 \cdot f(0)$

$\alpha = 2\sqrt{3} \cdot 4 - 0 = 8\sqrt{3}$

Therefore, $\alpha^2 = (8\sqrt{3})^2 = 64 \times 3 = 192$.

Answer: $192$

Let $u = x^2 + 1$, then $x^2 = u - 1$.

questions.q: If $\int\left(\frac{1-5 \cos ^{2} x}{\sin ^{5} x \cos ^{2} x}\right) d x=f(x)+\mathrm{C}$, where C is the constant of integration, then $f\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)-f\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$\int \frac{1 - 5\cos^2 x}{\sin^5 x \cos^2 x} dx = \int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x \cos^2 x} - 5\int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x}$

$= \int \frac{\sec^2 x \, dx}{\sin^5 x} - 5\int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x}$

By IBP:
$= \frac{\tan x}{\sin^5 x} - \int \left(-\frac{5}{\sin^6 x}\right) \cos x \cdot \tan x \, dx - 5\int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x}$

$= \frac{\tan x}{\sin^5 x} + C$

So $f(x) = \frac{\tan x}{\sin^5 x}$

$f\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) - f\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{2^5}{\sqrt{3}} - (\sqrt{2})^5 = \frac{32}{\sqrt{3}} - 4\sqrt{2} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}(8 - \sqrt{6})$

$\int \frac{1 - 5\cos^2 x}{\sin^5 x \cos^2 x} dx = \int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x \cos^2 x} - 5\int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x}$

$= \int \frac{\sec^2 x \, dx}{\sin^5 x} - 5\int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x}$

By IBP:
$= \frac{\tan x}{\sin^5 x} - \int \left(-\frac{5}{\sin^6 x}\right) \cos x \cdot \tan x \, dx - 5\int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x}$

$= \frac{\tan x}{\sin^5 x} + C$

questions.q: If $f(x)$ satisfies the relation $f(x)=e^{x}+\int_{0}^{1}\left(y+x e^{x}\right) f(y) d y$, then $e+f(0)$ is equal to $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution:
$f(x) = e^x + \displaystyle\int_0^1 (y + xe^x)f(y)\, dy$

Splitting the integral:
$f(x) = e^x + \displaystyle\int_0^1 yf(y)\, dy + xe^x \int_0^1 f(y)\, dy$

Let $A = \displaystyle\int_0^1 yf(y)\, dy$ and $B = \displaystyle\int_0^1 f(y)\, dy$

$\Rightarrow f(x) = (1 + Bx)e^x + A$

At $x = 0$: $f(0) = 1 + A$

Now compute $B$ using the expression for $f(y)$:
$B = \displaystyle\int_0^1 \left[(1 + By)e^y + A\right] dy$
$B = \displaystyle\int_0^1 e^y\, dy + B\int_0^1 ye^y\, dy + \int_0^1 A\, dy$

Evaluating each integral:
$\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^y\, dy = e - 1$
$\displaystyle\int_0^1 ye^y\, dy = [ye^y]_0^1 - \int_0^1 e^y\, dy = e - (e - 1) = 1$
$\displaystyle\int_0^1 A\, dy = A$

$\Rightarrow B = (e - 1) + B(1) + A$
$\Rightarrow 0 = e - 1 + A$
$\Rightarrow A = 1 - e$

$f(0) = 1 + A = 1 + (1 - e) = 2 - e$

$e + f(0) = e + (2 - e) = 2$

Answer: $2$

questions.q: Let a differentiable function $f$ satisfy the equation $\int_{0}^{36} f\left(\frac{t x}{36}\right) d t=4 \alpha f(x)$. If $y=f(x)$ is a standard parabola passing through the points $(2,1)$ and $(-4, \beta)$, then $\beta^{\alpha}$ is equal to $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution:
From $\int_0^{36} f\left(\frac{tx}{36}\right) dt = 4\alpha f(x)$, substitute $u = \frac{tx}{36}$ to get $\frac{36}{x} \int_0^x f(u) du = 4\alpha f(x)$.
Differentiating: $f(x) = \frac{\alpha}{9}[f(x) + xf'(x)]$, which simplifies to $(9-\alpha)f(x) = \alpha x f'(x)$.
This gives $\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} = \frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha x}$, integrating to $f(x) = Kx^{\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha}}$.
For f to be a standard parabola: $\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha} = 2 \Rightarrow \alpha = 3$.
Thus $f(x) = Kx^2$. Using point $(2,1)$: $K = \frac{1}{4}$, so $f(x) = \frac{x^2}{4}$.
At $(-4, \beta)$: $\beta = \frac{16}{4} = 4$.
Therefore $\beta^\alpha = 4^3 = 64$

questions.q:
The number of elements in the
set $\mathrm{S}=\left\{x: x \in[0,100]\right.$ and $\left.\int_{0}^{x} t^{2} \sin (x-t) \mathrm{d} t=x^{2}\right\}$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution:
Using $u = x - t$: $\int_0^x t^2 \sin(x-t)\,dt = \int_0^x (x-u)^2 \sin u\,du$.
Expanding and integrating term by term:
$= x^2(1-\cos x) - 2x(-x\cos x + \sin x) + (-x^2\cos x + 2x\sin x + 2\cos x - 2)$
$= x^2 + 2\cos x - 2$.
Setting equal to $x^2$: $2\cos x - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow \cos x = 1 \Rightarrow x = 2n\pi$.
In $[0, 100]$: $2n\pi \le 100 \Rightarrow n \le \frac{50}{\pi} \approx 15.9$.
So $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, 15$, giving $16$ elements.

questions.q: The value of the integral $\int_{\frac{\pi}{24}}^{\frac{5 \pi}{24}} \frac{\mathrm{~d} x}{1+\sqrt[3]{\tan 2 x}}$ is :
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_{\pi/24}^{5\pi/24} \frac{dx}{1+\sqrt[3]{\tan 2x}}$.
Apply King's rule ($x \to \pi/4 - x$):
$I = \int_{\pi/24}^{5\pi/24} \frac{dx}{1+\sqrt[3]{\cot 2x}} = \int_{\pi/24}^{5\pi/24} \frac{\sqrt[3]{\tan 2x}}{1+\sqrt[3]{\tan 2x}}dx$.
Adding: $2I = \int_{\pi/24}^{5\pi/24} dx = \frac{5\pi}{24} - \frac{\pi}{24} = \frac{\pi}{6}$.
$I = \frac{\pi}{12}$.

questions.q: Let $f(x)=[x]^{2}-[x+3]-3, x \in \mathbf{R}$, where [] is the greatest integer funtion. Then
questions.solution:
For $x \in [n, n+1)$ where $n$ is an integer, $[x] = n$ and $[x+3] = n+3$.
Thus $f(x) = n^2 - (n+3) - 3 = n^2 - n - 6 = (n-3)(n+2)$.
For $f(x) < 0$, we need $(n-3)(n+2) < 0$, which gives $-2 < n < 3$, i.e., $n \in \{-1, 0, 1, 2\}$.
This corresponds to $x \in [-1, 3)$.
We can verify:
For $n = -1$: $f = 1 - 2 - 3 = -4 < 0$
For $n = 0,1$: $f = -6 < 0$
For $n = 2$: $f = 4 - 5 - 3 = -4 < 0$
For $n = 3$: $f = 9 - 6 - 3 = 0$
For $n \geq 4$, $(n-3)(n+2) > 0$.
Therefore $f(x) < 0$ only for $x \in [-1, 3)$.

questions.q: Let $[\cdot]$ be the greatest integer function. If $\alpha=\int_{0}^{64}\left(x^{1 / 3}-\left[x^{1 / 3}\right]\right) \mathrm{d} x$, then $\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\alpha \pi}\left(\frac{\sin ^{2} \theta}{\sin ^{6} \theta+\cos ^{6} \theta}\right) \mathrm{d} \theta$ is equal to $\_\_\_\_$ .
questions.solution:
$\because \int_{0}^{64} x^{\frac{1}{3}} \, dx = \dfrac{3}{4} \left[ x^{\frac{4}{3}} \right]_{0}^{64} = 192$ &
$\int_{0}^{64} [x^{1/3}] \, dx = \int_{0}^{1} [x^{1/3}] \, dx + \int_{1}^{8} [x^{1/3}] \, dx + \int_{8}^{27} [x^{1/3}] \, dx + \int_{27}^{64} [x^{1/3}] \, dx = 156$
So $\alpha = 192 - 156 = 36$
Now $E = \dfrac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{36\pi} \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta} \, d\theta$
$= \dfrac{36}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\pi} \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta} \, d\theta$
$\Rightarrow E = \dfrac{36 \cdot 2}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta} \, d\theta$
Let $J = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta} \, d\theta$ ....(1)
Applying King
$J = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta} \, d\theta$ .....(2)
Now $2J = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{1}{\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta} \, d\theta$ (add (1) & (2))
$= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sec^6\theta}{\tan^6\theta + 1} \, d\theta$
$= \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{(1 + \lambda^2)}{\lambda^4 - \lambda^2 + 1} \, d\lambda$
$= \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1 + \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2}}{\lambda^2 - 1 + \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2}} \, d\lambda$
$= \pi$
$\Rightarrow J = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$
$\Rightarrow E = \dfrac{36 \cdot 2}{\pi} \times J = 36$

questions.q: If $\int_{0}^{1} 4 \cot ^{-1}\left(1-2 x+4 x^{2}\right) \mathrm{d} x=\mathrm{atan}^{-1}(2)-\mathrm{blog}_{\mathrm{e}}(5)$, where $\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b} \in \mathbf{N}$, then $(2 \mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b})$ is equal to $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution:
Let $I=\int_0^1 \cot ^{-1}\left(1-2 x+4 x^2\right) d x$
$I=\int_0^1\left(\cot ^{-1}(2 x-1)-\cot ^{-1}(2 x)\right) d x$

Applying king
$I=\int_0^1\left(-\cot ^{-1}(2 x-1)+\cot ^{-1}(2 x-2)\right) d x$

From (1) and (2)

$2 I=\int_0^1\left(\cot ^{-1}(2 x-2)-\cot ^{-1}(2 x)\right) d x$
$=\int_0^1 \cot ^{-1}(2 x-2) d x-\int_0^1 \cot ^{-1}(2 x) d x$

Applying King

$=\int_0^1 \cot ^{-1}(-2 x) d x-\int_0^1 \cot ^{-1}(2 x) d x$
$=\int_0^1\left(\pi-\cot ^{-1}(2 x)\right) d x-\int_0^1 \cot ^{-1}(2 x) d x$
$=\int_0^1\left(\pi-2 \cot ^{-1}(2 x)\right) d x$
$=\pi-2 \int_0^1\left(\cot ^{-1} 2 x\right) \cdot 1 d x$

By parts
$=\pi-2\left[\left(x \cot ^{-1} 2 x\right)_0^1+\int_0^1 \frac{2 x}{1+4 x^2} d x\right]$

Let $1+4 \mathrm{x}^2=\mathrm{t}$
$8 \mathrm{xdx}=\mathrm{dt}$
$=\pi-2\left[\cot ^{-1} 2+\frac{1}{4} \int_1^5 \frac{\mathrm{dt}}{\mathrm{t}}\right]$
$=\pi-2 \cot ^{-1} 2-\frac{1}{2} \ell \mathrm{n} 5$
$2 \mathrm{I}=2 \tan ^{-1} 2-\frac{1}{2} \ell \mathrm{n} 5$
$\Rightarrow 4 \mathrm{I}=4 \tan ^{-1} 2-\ell \mathrm{n} 5$
$\therefore 2 \mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}=8+1=9$

questions.q: The value of $\int_{-\pi / 6}^{\pi / 6}\left(\frac{\pi+4 x^{11}}{1-\sin (|x|+\pi / 6)}\right) d x$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Split: $\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \frac{\pi}{1 - \sin(|x| + \pi/6)} dx + \int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \frac{4x^{11}}{1 - \sin(|x| + \pi/6)} dx$.
Second integral = 0 (odd function over symmetric interval).
First integral: $2\pi \int_{0}^{\pi/6} \frac{1}{1 - \sin(x + \pi/6)} dx$.
Let $u = x + \pi/6$: $= 2\pi \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \frac{1}{1 - \sin u} du$.
$\frac{1}{1-\sin u} = \sec^2 u + \sec u \tan u$.
$= 2\pi [\tan u + \sec u]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} = 2\pi[(\sqrt{3}+2) - \sqrt{3}] = 4\pi$.

$\frac{1}{1-\sin u} = \sec^2 u + \sec u \tan u$.
$= 2\pi [\tan u + \sec u]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} = 2\pi[(\sqrt{3}+2) - \sqrt{3}] = 4\pi$.

questions.q: Let $f(x)$ be a positive function and $I_1=\int_{-\frac{1}{2}}^1 2 x f(2 x(1-2 x)) d x$ and $I_2=\int_{-1}^2 f(x(1-x)) d x$. Then the value of $\frac{I_2}{I_1}$ is equal to ________
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}_1=\int_{-\frac{1}{2}}^1 2 \mathrm{xf}(2 \mathrm{x}(1-2 \mathrm{x})) \mathrm{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{t} \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{dx}=\mathrm{dt} \quad \Rightarrow \mathrm{I}_1=\frac{1}{2} \int_{-1}^2 \mathrm{tf}(\mathrm{t}(1-\mathrm{t})) \mathrm{dt} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}_1=\int_{-1}^2(1-\mathrm{t}) \mathrm{f}(1-\mathrm{t})(1-(1-\mathrm{t})) \mathrm{dt} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}_1=\int_{-1}^2 \mathrm{f}\left(\mathrm{t}(1-\mathrm{t}) \mathrm{dt}-\int_{-1}^2 \mathrm{tf}(\mathrm{t}(1-\mathrm{t}) \mathrm{dt}\right. \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}_1=\mathrm{I}_2-2 \mathrm{I}_1 \\ & \Rightarrow 4 \mathrm{I}_1=\mathrm{I}_2 \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{I}_2}{\mathrm{I}_1}=4\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The integral $\int_{-1}^{\frac{3}{2}}\left(\left|\pi^2 x \sin (\pi x)\right|\right) d x$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Let, $\mathrm{I}=\pi^2 \int_{-1}^{3 / 2}|\mathrm{x} \sin \pi \mathrm{x}| \mathrm{dx}$
$\begin{aligned}
& =\pi^2\left\{\int_{-1}^1 \mathrm{x} \sin \pi \mathrm{xdx}-\int_1^{3 / 2} \mathrm{x} \sin \pi \mathrm{xdx}\right\} \\ & =\pi^2\left\{2 \int_0^1 \mathrm{x} \sin \pi \mathrm{xdx}-\int_{-1}^{3 / 2} \mathrm{x} \sin \pi \mathrm{xdx}\right\}
\end{aligned}$
Consider
$\begin{aligned}
& \int \mathrm{x} \sin \pi \mathrm{xdx} \\ & -\mathrm{x} \cdot \frac{1}{\pi} \cos \pi \mathrm{x}+\int 1 \cdot \frac{1}{\pi} \cos \pi \mathrm{xdx} \\ & =-\frac{\mathrm{x}}{\pi} \cos \pi \mathrm{x}+\frac{\sin \pi \mathrm{x}}{\pi^2}
\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{I} & =\pi^2\left\{2\left(-\frac{\mathrm{x}}{\pi} \cos \pi \mathrm{x}+\frac{\sin \pi \mathrm{x}}{\pi^2}\right)_0^1-\left(-\frac{\mathrm{x}}{\pi} \cos \pi \mathrm{x}+\frac{\sin \pi \mathrm{x}}{\pi^2}\right)_1^{3 / 2}\right\} \\ & =\pi^2\left\{\frac{2}{\pi}-\left(-\frac{1}{\pi^2}-\frac{1}{\pi}\right)\right\} \\ & =\pi^2\left\{\frac{3}{\pi}+\frac{1}{\pi^2}\right\} \\ & =3 \pi+1\end{aligned}$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}=\int_{-1}^1 \frac{(1+\sqrt{|-\mathrm{x}|-(-\mathrm{x})}) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{x}}+(\sqrt{|-\mathrm{x}|-(-\mathrm{x})}) \mathrm{e}^{-(-\mathrm{x})}}{\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{x}}+\mathrm{e}^{-(-\mathrm{x})}} \mathrm{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{I}=\int_{-1}^1 \frac{(1+\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|+\mathrm{x}}) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{x}}+(\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|+\mathrm{x}}) \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}}{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}+\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}} \mathrm{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}=\int_{-1}^1 \frac{(1+\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|+\mathrm{x}}+\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|-\mathrm{x}})\left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}+\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{x}}\right)}{\left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}+\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{x}}\right)} \mathrm{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}=\int_{-1}^1(1+\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|+\mathrm{x}}+\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|-\mathrm{x}}) \mathrm{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}=2 \int_0^1(1+\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|+\mathrm{x}}+\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|-\mathrm{x}}) \mathrm{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}=2 \int_0^1(1+\sqrt{2 \mathrm{x}}+\sqrt{0}) \mathrm{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{I}=\int_0^1(1+\sqrt{2 \mathrm{x}}) \mathrm{dx}=\left[\mathrm{x}+\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3} \mathrm{x}^{3 / 2}\right]_0^1 \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{I}=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3}+1\end{aligned}$

where [$\cdot]$ is the greatest integer function, then $\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{q}+\mathrm{r}$ is equal to
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \log _4 \log _6\left(3+4 x-x^2\right) > 0 \\ & \log _6\left(3+4 x-x^2\right) > 1\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & 3+4 x-x^2 > 6 \\ & x^2-4 x+3 < 0 \\ & (x-1)(x-3) < 0 \\ & x \in(1,3) \\ & \text{ so } a=1 \& b=3 \\ & \Rightarrow \int_0^2\left[x^2\right] d x=? \\ & I=\int_0^1\left[x^2\right] d x+\int_1^{\sqrt{2}}\left[x^2\right] d x+\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{3}}\left[x^2\right] d x+\int_{\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{4}}\left[x^2\right] d x \\ & =0+|x|_1^{\sqrt{2}}+2|x|_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{3}}+3|x|_{\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{4}}\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & =(\sqrt{2}-1)+2(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2})+3(2-\sqrt{3}) \\ & =5-\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{3} \Rightarrow \mathrm{p}+\mathrm{q}+\mathrm{r}=10\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & x^2=2 y \& y=2 x+6 \\ & x^2=4 x+12\end{aligned}$
$\left.x^2-4 x-12=0 \Rightarrow \begin{gathered}x=6 \\ y=18\end{gathered} \right\rvert\, \begin{gathered}\text{ if } x=-2 \\ y=2\end{gathered}$
$\therefore(6,18) \&(-2,2)$
Here $(6,18)$ Rejected because $(a, b)$ lies in $2^{\text{nd }}$ quadrant
$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \mathrm{a}=-2 \& \mathrm{~b}=2 \\ & \therefore \mathrm{I}=\int_{-2}^2 \frac{9 \mathrm{x}^2}{1+5^{\mathrm{x}}} \mathrm{dx}=\int_{-2}^2 \frac{9 \cdot 5^{\mathrm{x}} \cdot \mathrm{x}^2}{1+5^{\mathrm{x}}} \mathrm{dx} \\ & \therefore 2 \mathrm{I}=\int_{-2}^2 9 \mathrm{x}^2 \mathrm{dx}=18 \int_0^2 \mathrm{x}^2 \mathrm{dx}=18\left(\frac{\mathrm{x}^3}{3}\right)_0^2 \\ & 2 \mathrm{I}=48 \\ & \therefore \mathrm{I}=24\end{aligned}$

questions.q: $4 \int_0^1\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3+x^2}+\sqrt{1+x^2}}\right) d x-3 \log _e(\sqrt{3})$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & 4 \int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{3+\mathrm{x}^2}+\sqrt{1+\mathrm{x}^2}} \mathrm{dx}-3 \ln \sqrt{3} \\ & =4 \int_0^1 \frac{\sqrt{3+\mathrm{x}^2}-\sqrt{1+\mathrm{x}^2}}{\left(3+\mathrm{x}^2\right)-\left(1-\mathrm{x}^2\right)} \mathrm{dx}-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3 \\ & = \\ & 2\left[\left\{\frac{\mathrm{x}}{2} \sqrt{3+\mathrm{x}^2}+\frac{3}{2} \ln \left(\mathrm{x}+\sqrt{3+\mathrm{x}^2}\right)\right\}_0^1\right. \\ & \left.\quad-\left\{\frac{\mathrm{x}}{2} \sqrt{1+\mathrm{x}^2}+\frac{1}{2} \ln \left(\mathrm{x}+\sqrt{1+\mathrm{x}^2}\right)\right\}_0^1\right]-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}= & 2\left[\left\{\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{4}+\frac{3}{2} \ln (1+\sqrt{4})\right\}-\left\{0+\frac{3}{2} \ln \sqrt{3}\right\}\right. \\ & \left.-\left\{\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{2}+\frac{1}{2} \ln (1+\sqrt{2})\right\}+\left\{0+\frac{1}{2}(0)\right\}\right]-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & =2\left[1+\frac{3}{2} \ln 3-\frac{3}{4} \ln 3-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{1}{2} \ln (1+\sqrt{2})\right]-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3 \\ & =2+3 \ln 3-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3-\sqrt{2}-\ln (1+\sqrt{2})-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3 \\ & =2-\sqrt{2}-\ln (1+\sqrt{2})\end{aligned}$

questions.solution: $f^{\prime}(x)=x\left(x^2-9 x+20\right), x \in(1,5) =(x-4) x(x-5) \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow f^{\prime}(x)>0 \forall x \in(1,4) \\ & \Rightarrow f^{\prime}(x) < 0 \forall x \in(4,5) \\ & \Rightarrow f(x) \text{ increasing$ in $}(1,4) \\ & \quad f(x) \text{ decreasing in }(4,5) \\ & \Rightarrow \text{ critical points to check: }\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & x=1,4,5 \\ & f(x)=\int_0^x\left(t^3-9 t^2+20 t\right) d t \\ & =\frac{t^4}{4}-3 t^3+\left.10 t^2\right|_0 ^x=\frac{x^4}{4}-3 x^3+10 x^2 \\ & f(1)=\frac{1}{4}-3+10=\frac{29}{4} \\ & f(4)=4^3-3.4^3+10.4^2=-2.4^3+10.4^2=32 \\ & f(5)=\frac{5^4}{4}-3.5^3+10.25=\frac{5^4}{4}-125=\frac{125}{4}\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \text{ Range } \Rightarrow\left[\frac{29}{4}, 32\right] \Rightarrow 4(\alpha+\beta)=128+29 \\ & =157\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
Let $I=24 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\sin \left|4 x-\frac{\pi}{2}\right|+[2 \sin x]\right) d x$   ...(i)
Now $\left|4 x-\frac{\pi}{12}\right|= \begin{cases}-4 x+\frac{\pi}{12} & ; x < \frac{\pi}{48} \\ 4 x-\frac{\pi}{12} & ; \quad x \geq \frac{\pi}{48}\end{cases} \therefore$ from $(\mathrm{i}) \begin{aligned} & I=24 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{48}}-\sin \left(4 x-\frac{\pi}{12}\right) d x+\int_{\frac{\pi}{48}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \sin \left(4 x-\frac{\pi}{12}\right) \\ & +\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}[2 \sin x] d x+\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}[2 \sin x] d x \\ & I=24\left[\frac{\left(1-\cos \frac{\pi}{12}\right)}{4}-\frac{\left(-\cos \frac{\pi}{12}-1\right)}{4}\right)+\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{\pi}{6} \\ & I=24\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{\pi}{6} \\ & I=2 \pi+12=2 \pi+\alpha \text{ (from above) } \\ & \therefore \quad \alpha=12\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The integral \(80 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\frac{\sin \theta+\cos \theta}{9+16 \sin 2 \theta}\right) d \theta\) is equal to :
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & I=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\frac{\sin \theta+\cos \theta}{9-16 \sin 2 \theta}\right) d \theta \\ & \text{ Take } \sin \theta-\cos \theta=t \\ & (\cos \theta+\sin \theta) d \theta=d t \\ & (\sin \theta-\cos \theta)^2=t^2 \\ & \Rightarrow \sin 2 \theta=1-t^2 \\ & \theta=0 \rightarrow t=-1 \\ & \quad \theta=\frac{\pi}{4} \rightarrow t=0 \\ & I=\int_{-1}^0 \frac{d t}{9+16\left(1-t^2\right)} \\ & =\frac{1}{16} \int_{-1}^0 \frac{d t}{25} \frac{16}{16}-t^2 \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\left[\frac{1}{10} \log _{\left\lvert\, \frac{5+4 t}{}\right.}^{5-4 t}\right]_{-1}^0 \\ & =\frac{1}{40}\left[0+\log _e 9\right] \\ & I=\frac{\log _e 9}{40} \\ & 80 I=2 \log _e 9 \\ & 80 I=4 \log _e 3\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Let \(f:(0, $\infty) \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ be a twice differentiable function. If for some \($\mathrm{a} \neq$0, \int_0^1 f(\lambda x) $\mathrm{d} \lambda=\mathrm{a}$f(x), f(1)=1\) and \(f(16)=$\frac{1}{8}$, then \(16-f^{\prime}$\left(\frac{1}{16}\right)$ is equal to _______.
questions.solution:
Given, $\int_0^1 f(\lambda x) d \lambda=a f(x)$
Let $\lambda x=u d \lambda=\frac{1}{x} d u \therefore$ From (1) $\frac{1}{x} \int_0^x f(u) d u=a f(x) \Rightarrow \int_0^x f(u) d u=\operatorname{axf}(x)$
Differentiate both sides
$\begin{aligned}
& f(x)=a\left(x f^{\prime}(x)+f(x)\right) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad f(x)=a x f^{\prime}(x)+a f(x) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad(1-a) f(x)=a x f^{\prime}(x) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}=\frac{(1-a)}{a} \cdot \frac{1}{x}
\end{aligned}$
Integrate both side w.r.t. ( $x$ )
$\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad \int \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)} d x=\frac{(1-a)}{a} \int \frac{1}{x} d x \\
& \Rightarrow \ln f(x)=\left(\frac{1-a}{a}\right) \ln x+c
\end{aligned}$
Now at $x=1 f(1)=1 \Rightarrow c=0$
Also given $f(16)=\frac{1}{8} \begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad \frac{1}{8}=(16)^{\frac{1-a}{a}} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 2^{-3}=2^{\frac{4-4 a}{a}} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad-3=\frac{4-4 a}{a} \\
& \Rightarrow-3 a=4-4 a \\
& \Rightarrow a=4 \\
& \therefore \quad f(x)=x^{-3 / 4} \\
& f(x)=\frac{-3}{4} x^{-\frac{7}{4}}
\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \text{ Put } x=\frac{1}{16} \\ & f^{\prime}\left(\frac{1}{16}\right)=\frac{-3}{4}\left(\frac{1}{16}\right)^{-7 / 4}=\frac{-3}{4} \cdot 2^{-4 x\left(\frac{-7}{4}\right)}=-96 \\ & \therefore \quad 16-f^{\prime}\left(\frac{1}{16}\right) \Rightarrow 16-(-96)=112\end{aligned}$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \int_0^x t f(t) d t=x^2 f(x) \\ & \Rightarrow \quad x f(x)=2 x f(x)+x^2 f^{\prime}(x) \\ & \Rightarrow x^2 \cdot f^{\prime}(x)=-x f(x) \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}=-\frac{1}{x} \\ & \\ & \quad \int \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x) d x}=-\int \frac{1}{x} d x \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \ln f(x)=-\ln x+C \\ & \\ & \quad f(2)=3 \Rightarrow \ln 3=-\ln 2+C \\ & \quad C=\ln 6 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad f(x)=\frac{6}{x} \Rightarrow f(6)=1\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Let for $f(x)=7 \tan ^8 x+7 \tan ^6 x-3 \tan ^4 x-3 \tan ^2 x, \quad \mathrm{I}_1=\int_0^{\pi / 4} f(x) \mathrm{d} x$ and $\mathrm{I}_2=\int_0^{\pi / 4} x f(x) \mathrm{d} x$. Then $7 \mathrm{I}_1+12 \mathrm{I}_2$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} f(x) & =7 \tan ^8 x+7 \tan ^6 x-3 \tan ^4 x-3 \tan ^2 x \\ & =7 \tan ^6 x\left(1+\tan ^2 x\right)-3 \tan ^2 x\left(1+\tan ^2 x\right) \\ & =\left(7 \tan ^6 x-3 \tan ^2 x\right)\left(1+\tan ^2 x\right) \\ & =\left(7 \tan ^6 x-3 \tan ^2 x\right) \sec ^2 x \\ l_1= & \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} f(x) d x=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(7 \tan ^6 x-3 \tan ^2 x\right) \sec ^2 x d x \\ & =\left.\left(\frac{7 \tan ^7 x}{7}-\frac{3 \tan ^3 x}{3}\right)\right|_0 ^{\frac{\pi}{4}}=1-1=0\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}
I_2= & \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} x f(x) d x=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} x\left(7 \tan ^6 x-3 \tan ^2 x\right) \sec ^2 x d x \\
& =\left.x\left(\tan ^7 x-\tan ^3 x\right)\right|_0 ^{\frac{\pi}{4}}-\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} 1 \cdot\left(\tan ^7 x-\tan ^3 x\right) d x \\
& =0-\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \tan ^3 x\left(\tan ^2 x-1\right)\left(\tan ^2 x+1\right) d x \\
& =\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\tan ^3 x-\tan ^5 x\right) \sec ^2 x d x=\frac{\tan ^4 x}{4}-\left.\frac{\tan ^6 x}{6}\right|_0 ^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\
& =\frac{1}{12}
\end{aligned}$

Hence $7 I_1+12 I_2=1$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \sqrt{1-\left(y^{\prime}(x)\right)^2}=y(x) \\ & 1-\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2=y^2 \\ & \left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2=1-y^2\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \frac{d y}{\sqrt{1-y^2}}=d x \text{$ OR $} \frac{d y}{\sqrt{1-y^2}}=-d x \\ & \Rightarrow \sin ^{-1} y=x+c, \sin ^{-1} y=-x+c \\ & x=0, y=0 \Rightarrow c=0 \\ & \sin ^{-1} y=x, \text{ as } y \geq 0 \\ & \sin x=y \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=\cos x \\ & \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=-\sin x \\ & \Rightarrow-\sin x+\sin x+1=1\end{aligned}$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & I=\int_{-1}^2 \log _e\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right) d x \\ & =x \log _e\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)-\int_{-1}^2\left(\frac{1+\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}}{x+\sqrt{x^2+1}}\right) d x \\ & =x \log _e\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)-\int_{-1}^2 \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} d x\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & =x \log _e\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)-\left.\sqrt{x^2+1}\right|_{-1} ^2 \\ & =\left(2 \log _e(2+\sqrt{5})-\sqrt{5}\right) \\ & -\left(-\log _e(-1+\sqrt{2})-\sqrt{2}\right) \\ & =\log _e(2+\sqrt{5})^2-\sqrt{5}+\log _e(\sqrt{2}-1)+\sqrt{2} \\ & =\log _e(2+\sqrt{5})^2-\sqrt{5}+\log _e(\sqrt{2}-1)+\sqrt{2}\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & =\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{5}+\log _e\left(\frac{(2+\sqrt{5})^2}{\sqrt{2+1}}\right) \\ & =\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{5}+\log _e\left(\frac{9+4 \sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{2+1}}\right)\end{aligned}$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \int_\alpha^{\log 4} \frac{\mathrm{dx}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}-1}}=\frac{\pi}{6} \\ & \text{ Let } \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}-1=\mathrm{t}^2 \\ & \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}} \mathrm{dx}=2 \mathrm{t} \mathrm{dt} \\ & =\int \frac{2 \mathrm{dt}}{\mathrm{t}^2+1} \\ & =2 \tan ^{-1} \mathrm{t} \\ & =\left.2 \tan ^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}-1}\right)\right|_\alpha ^{\log _{\mathrm{e}^4} \\ & =2\left[\tan ^{-1} \sqrt{3}-\tan ^{-1} \sqrt{\mathrm{e}^\alpha-1}\right]=\frac{\pi}{6} \\ & =\frac{\pi}{3}-\tan ^{-1} \sqrt{\mathrm{e}^\alpha-1}=\frac{\pi}{12} \\ & \Rightarrow \tan ^{-1} \sqrt{\mathrm{e}^\alpha-1}=\frac{\pi}{4} \\ & \mathrm{e}^\alpha=2 \quad \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha}=\frac{1}{2} \\ & \mathrm{x}^2-\left(2+\frac{1}{2}\right) \mathrm{x}+1=0 \\ & 2 \mathrm{x}^2-5 \mathrm{x}+2=0\end{aligned}$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & I_n=\int_0^1\left(1-x^k\right)^n \cdot 1 d x \\ & I_n=\left(1-x^k\right)^n \cdot x-n k \int_0^1\left(1-x^k\right)^{n-1} \cdot x^{k-1} \cdot d x \\ & I_n=n k \int_0^1\left[\left(1-x^k\right)^n-\left(1-x^k\right)^{n-1}\right] d x \\ & I_n=n k I_n-n k I_n \\ & \frac{I_n}{I_{n-1}}=\frac{n k}{n k+1} \\ & \frac{I_{21}}{I_{20}}=\frac{21 k}{1+21 k} \\ & =\frac{147}{148} \Rightarrow k=7\end{aligned}$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \int_0^3\left[x^2\right] d x+\int_0^3\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right] d x \\ & =\int_0^1 0 d x+\int_1^{12} 1 d x+\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{3}} 2 d x\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & +\int_{\sqrt{3}}^2 3 \mathrm{dx}+\int_2^{\sqrt{5}} 4 \mathrm{dx}+\int_{\sqrt{5}}^{\sqrt{6}} 5 \mathrm{dx} \\ & +\int_{\sqrt{6}}^{\sqrt{7}} 6 \mathrm{dx}+\int_{\sqrt{7}}^{\sqrt{8}} 7 \mathrm{dx}+\int_{\sqrt{8}}^3 8 \mathrm{dx} \\ & +\int_0^{\sqrt{2}} 0 \mathrm{dx}+\int_{\sqrt{2}}^2 1 \mathrm{dx} \\ & +\int_2^{\sqrt{6}} 2 \mathrm{dx}+\int_{\sqrt{6}}^{\sqrt{8}} 3 \mathrm{dx}+\int_{\sqrt{8}}^3 4 \mathrm{dx}=31-6 \sqrt{2}-\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{5} \\ & -2 \sqrt{6}-\sqrt{7} \\ & \mathrm{a}=31 \quad \mathrm{~b}=-6 \quad \mathrm{c}=-2 \\ & \mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}+\mathrm{c}=31-6-2=23\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
$f(t)=\int_0^\pi \frac{2 x}{1-\cos ^2 t \sin ^2 x} d x$ .....(1)
$=2 \int_0^\pi \frac{(\pi-x) d x}{1-\cos ^2 \sin ^2 x}$ .....(2)
$\begin{aligned}
& 2 f(t)=2 \int_0^\pi \frac{\pi}{1-\cos ^2 \sin ^2 x} d x \\
& f(t)=\int_0^\pi \frac{\pi}{1-\cos ^2 t \sin ^2 x} d x
\end{aligned}$
divide \& by $\cos ^2 \mathrm{x} \begin{aligned}
& f(t)=\pi \int_0^\pi \frac{\sec ^2 x d x}{\sec ^2 x-\cos ^2 t^2 x} \\
& f(t)=2 \pi \int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{\sec ^2 x d x}{\sec ^2 x-\cos ^2 t^2 \tan ^2 x} \\
& \tan x=z \\
& \sec ^2 x d x=d z \\
& f(t)=2 \pi \int_0^{\infty} \frac{d z}{1+\sin ^2 t \cdot z^2} \\
& =\frac{\pi^2}{\sin t}
\end{aligned}$
Then $\int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{\pi^2}{f(t)} d t \begin{aligned}

questions.question: If $f(t)=\int_0^\pi \frac{2 x \mathrm{~d} x}{1-\cos ^2 \mathrm{t} \sin ^2 x}, 0 < \mathrm{t} < \pi$, then the value of $\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\pi^2 \mathrm{dt}}{f(\mathrm{t})}$ equals_________
questions.explanation:
$f(t)=\int_0^\pi \frac{2 x}{1-\cos ^2 t \sin ^2 x} d x$ .....(1)
$=2 \int_0^\pi \frac{(\pi-x) d x}{1-\cos ^2 \sin ^2 x}$ .....(2)
$\begin{aligned}
& 2 f(t)=2 \int_0^\pi \frac{\pi}{1-\cos ^2 \sin ^2 x} d x \\
& f(t)=\int_0^\pi \frac{\pi}{1-\cos ^2 t \sin ^2 x} d x
\end{aligned}$
divide \& by $\cos ^2 \mathrm{x} \begin{aligned}
& f(t)=\pi \int_0^\pi \frac{\sec ^2 x d x}{\sec ^2 x-\cos ^2 t^2 x} \\
& f(t)=2 \pi \int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{\sec ^2 x d x}{\sec ^2 x-\cos ^2 t^2 \tan ^2 x} \\
& \tan x=z \\
& \sec ^2 x d x=d z \\
& f(t)=2 \pi \int_0^{\infty} \frac{d z}{1+\sin ^2 t \cdot z^2} \\
& =\frac{\pi^2}{\sin t}
\end{aligned}$
Then $\int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{\pi^2}{f(t)} d t \begin{aligned}
& =\int_0^{\pi / 2} \sin t d t \\
& =1
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The value of $\int_{-\pi}^\pi \frac{2 y(1+\sin y)}{1+\cos ^2 y} d y$ is :
questions.solution:

$=0+2.2 \int_0^\pi y\left(\frac{\sin y}{1+\cos ^2 y}\right) d y \begin{aligned} & I=4 \int_0^\pi \frac{y \sin y}{1+\cos ^2 y} d y \\ & I=4 \int_0^\pi \frac{(\pi-y) \sin y}{1+\cos ^2 y} d y \\ & 2 I=4 \int_0^\pi \frac{\pi \sin y}{1+\cos ^2 y} d y \\ & I=2 \pi \int_0^\pi \frac{\sin y}{1+\cos ^2 y} d y \\ & =2 \pi\left(-\tan ^{-1}(\cos y)\right)_0^\pi \\ & =-2 \pi\left[\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right] \\ & =-2 \pi\left[-\frac{2 \pi}{4}\right]=\pi^2\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The integral $\int_0^{\pi / 4} \frac{136 \sin x}{3 \sin x+5 \cos x} d x$ is equal to :
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & I=\int_0^{\pi / 4} \frac{136 \sin x}{3 \sin x+5 \cos x} d x \\ & 136 \sin x=A(3 \sin x+5 \cos x)+B(3 \cos x-5 \sin x) \\ & 136=3 A-5 B...(i) \\ & 0=5 A+3 B...(ii)\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & 3 \mathrm{~B}=-5 \mathrm{~A} \Rightarrow \mathrm{B}=-\frac{5}{3} \mathrm{~A} \\ & 136=3 \mathrm{~A}-5\left(-\frac{5}{3} \mathrm{~A}\right) \\ & 136=3 \mathrm{~A}+\frac{25}{3} \mathrm{~A} \\ & 136=\frac{34 \mathrm{~A}}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{A}=\frac{136 \times 3}{34}=12 \\ & \mathrm{~B}=\frac{-5}{3}(12)=-20\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & I=\int_0^{\pi / 4} \frac{A(3 \sin x+5 \cos x)}{3 \sin x+5 \cos x}+\int_0^{\pi / 4} \frac{B(3 \cos x-5 \sin x)}{3 \sin x+5 \cos x} \\ & =A(x)_0^{\pi / 4}+B[\ln (3 \sin x+5 \cos x)]_0^{\pi / 4} \\ & =12\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-20 \ln \left(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\right)-\ln (0+5) \\ & =3 \pi-20 \ln 4 \sqrt{2}+20 \ln 5 \\ & =3 \pi-20 \times \frac{5}{2} \ln 2+20 \ln 5 \\ & =3 \pi-50 \ln 2+20 \ln 5\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The value of ${∫}_{0}^{1}\left(2{x}^{3} - 3{x}^{2} - x + 1\right)\dfrac{1}{3}dx$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
$I = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\left(2{x}^{3} - 3{x}^{2} - x + 1\right)\dfrac{1}{3}dx$

Using $\mathop{∫}_{0}^{2a}f\left(x\right)dx = 0$ when$f\left(2a - x\right) = - f\left(x\right)$

Now, finding $f\left(1 - x\right)$ we get,

$⇒ I = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\left(2{\left(1 - x\right)}^{3} - 3{\left(1 - x\right)}^{2} - \left(1 - x\right) + 1\right)\dfrac{1}{3}dx$

$⇒ I = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\left(2\left(1 - {x}^{3} - 3x + 3{x}^{2}\right) - 3{\left(1 + {x}^{2} - 2x\right)}^{2} - \left(1 - x\right) + 1\right)\dfrac{1}{3}dx$

$⇒ I = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\left(2 - 2{x}^{3} - 6x + 6{x}^{2} - 3 - 3{x}^{2} + 6x - 1 + x + 1\right)\dfrac{1}{3}dx$

$⇒ I = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\left(- 2{x}^{3} + 3{x}^{2} + x - 1\right)\dfrac{1}{3}dx$

$⇒ I = - I$

$⇒ f\left(1 - x\right) = - f\left(x\right)$

$∴ I = 0$

$⇒ I = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\left(2\left(1 - {x}^{3} - 3x + 3{x}^{2}\right) - 3{\left(1 + {x}^{2} - 2x\right)}^{2} - \left(1 - x\right) + 1\right)\dfrac{1}{3}dx$

questions.q: If $\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}\cos^{4}xdx = a\pi + b\sqrt{3}$, where $a$ and $b$ are rational numbers, then $9a + 8b$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Let,  $I = {∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}\cos^{4}x d x$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{1}{4}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}{\left(2\cos^{2}x\right)}^{2} d x$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{1}{4}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}{\left(1 + cos2x\right)}^{2} d x$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{1}{4}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}\left(1 + \cos^{2}2x + 2cos2x\right) d x$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{1}{4}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}\left(1 + 2cos2x\right) d x + \dfrac{1}{8}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}2\cos^{2}2xdx$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{1}{4}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}\left(1 + 2cos2x\right) d x + \dfrac{1}{8}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}\left(1 + cos4x\right)dx$

$⇒ I = {\left[\dfrac{1}{4}\left(x + sin2x\right) + \dfrac{1}{8}\left(x + \dfrac{sin4x}{4}\right)\right]}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} + sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) + \dfrac{1}{8}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3}}{4}\right)$

$⇒ I = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{12} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{8}\right) + \left(\dfrac{\pi}{24} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{64}\right)$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{\pi}{8} + \dfrac{7\sqrt{3}}{64}$

So, on comparing with given value we get, $a = \dfrac{1}{8}, b = \dfrac{7}{64}$

$⇒ 9a + 8b = \dfrac{9}{8} + \dfrac{7}{8}$

$⇒ 9a + 8b = \dfrac{16}{8}$

$⇒ 9a + 8b = 2$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $f: \left(0, \infty\right) \to R$ and $F\left(x\right) = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{x}tf\left(t\right)dt$. If $F\left({x}^{2}\right) = {x}^{4} + {x}^{5},$ then $\mathop{∑}_{r = 1}^{12}f\left({r}^{2}\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Given: 

$F\left(x\right) = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{x}t ⋅ f\left(t\right)dt$

Now, applying Newton Leibnitz Theorem we get,

${F}^{'}\left(x\right) = x ⋅ f\left(x\right)$

 And $F\left({x}^{2}\right) = {x}^{4} + {x}^{5}$

Let ${x}^{2} = t$

$⇒ F\left(t\right) = {t}^{2} + t\dfrac{5}{2}$

$⇒ {F}^{'}\left(t\right) = 2t + \dfrac{5}{2}t\dfrac{3}{2} \left\{\text{as}{F}^{'}\left(x\right) = x ⋅ f\left(x\right)\right\}$

$⇒ t ⋅ f\left(t\right) = 2t + \dfrac{5}{2}t\dfrac{3}{2}$

$⇒ f\left(t\right) = 2 + \dfrac{5}{2}t\dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{r = 1}^{12}f\left({r}^{2}\right) = \mathop{∑}_{r = 1}^{12}2 + \dfrac{5}{2}r$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{r = 1}^{12}f\left({r}^{2}\right) = 24 + \dfrac{5}{2}\left[\dfrac{12\left(13\right)}{2}\right]$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{r = 1}^{12}f\left({r}^{2}\right) = 219$

questions.q: The value of the integral $\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}\dfrac{xdx}{\sin^{4}\left(2x\right) + \cos^{4}\left(2x\right)}$ equals:
questions.solution:
Let, $\mathop{I = ∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}\dfrac{xdx}{\sin^{4}\left(2x\right) + \cos^{4}\left(2x\right)}$

Let, $2x = t$ then $dx = \dfrac{1}{2}dt$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{1}{4}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{tdt}{\sin^{4}t + \cos^{4}t}$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{1}{4}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - t\right)dt}{\sin^{4}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - t\right) + \cos^{4}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - t\right)}$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{1}{4}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{\dfrac{\pi}{2}dt}{\sin^{4}t + \cos^{4}t} - I$

$⇒ 2I = \dfrac{\pi}{8}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{dt}{\sin^{4}t + \cos^{4}t}$

$⇒ 2I = \dfrac{\pi}{8}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{{sec}^{4}tdt}{\tan^{4}t + 1}$

Let, $tant = y$ then ${sec}^{2}tdt = dy$

$⇒ 2I = \dfrac{\pi}{8}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\infty}\dfrac{\left(1 + {y}^{2}\right)dy}{1 + {y}^{4}}$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{\pi}{16}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\infty}\dfrac{1 + \dfrac{1}{{y}^{2}}}{{y}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{{y}^{2}}}dy$

Putting, $y - \dfrac{1}{y} = p$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{\pi}{16}\mathop{∫}_{- \infty}^{\infty}\dfrac{dp}{{p}^{2} + {\left(\sqrt{2}\right)}^{2}}$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{\pi}{16\sqrt{2}}{\left[\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{p}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right]}_{- \infty}^{\infty}$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{{\pi}^{2}}{16\sqrt{2}}$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}{\pi}^{2}}{32}$
questions.question: The value of the integral $\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}\dfrac{xdx}{\sin^{4}\left(2x\right) + \cos^{4}\left(2x\right)}$ equals:

Let, $tant = y$ then ${sec}^{2}tdt = dy$

questions.solution:
Given: $I = \mathop{∫}_{- \dfrac{\pi}{2}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{8\sqrt{2}cosx}{\left(1 + {e}^{sinx}\right)\left(1 + \sin^{4}x\right)}dx . . . \left(i\right)$

Applying ${∫}_{a}^{b}f\left(x\right) d x = {∫}_{a}^{b}f\left(a + b - x\right) d x$ rule we get,

$⇒ I = \mathop{∫}_{- \dfrac{\pi}{2}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{8\sqrt{2}cosx\left({e}^{sinx}\right)}{\left(1 + {e}^{sinx}\right)\left(1 + \sin^{4}x\right)}dx . . . \left(ii\right)$

Adding $\left(i\right)\text{and}\left(ii\right)$

$⇒ 2I = \mathop{∫}_{- \dfrac{\pi}{2}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{8\sqrt{2}cosx}{1 + \sin^{4}x}dx$

$⇒ I = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{8\sqrt{2}cosx}{1 + \sin^{4}x}dx$

Putting, $sinx = t$

$⇒ I = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\dfrac{8\sqrt{2}}{1 + {t}^{4}}dx$

$⇒ I = 4\sqrt{2}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\left(\dfrac{1 + \dfrac{1}{{t}^{2}}}{{t}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{{t}^{2}}} - \dfrac{1 - \dfrac{1}{{t}^{2}}}{{t}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{{t}^{2}}}\right)dt$

$⇒ I = 4\sqrt{2}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\left(\dfrac{1 + \dfrac{1}{{t}^{2}}}{{\left(t - \dfrac{1}{t}\right)}^{2} + 2} - \dfrac{\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{{t}^{2}}\right)}{{\left(t + \dfrac{1}{t}\right)}^{2} - 2}\right)dt$

Let $t - \dfrac{1}{t} = z$ and $t + \dfrac{1}{t} = k$

$⇒ I = 4\sqrt{2}\left[\mathop{∫}_{- \infty}^{0}\dfrac{dz}{{z}^{2} + 2} - \mathop{∫}_{\infty}^{2}\dfrac{dk}{{k}^{2} - 2}\right]$

$⇒ I = 4\sqrt{2}{\left[\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan^{- 1}\dfrac{z}{\sqrt{2}}\right]}_{- \infty}^{0} - {\left[\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}ln\left(\dfrac{k - \sqrt{2}}{k + \sqrt{2}}\right)\right]}_{\infty}^{2}$

$⇒ I = 4\sqrt{2}\left[\dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\left[ln\dfrac{2 - \sqrt{2}}{2 + \sqrt{2}}\right]\right]$

$⇒ I = 2\pi + 2log\left(3 + 2\sqrt{2}\right)$

Comparing this value with $\left[\alpha\pi + \beta{\log}_{e}\left(3 + 2\sqrt{2}\right)\right]$

$⇒ \alpha = 2$ and $\beta = 2$

$⇒ {\alpha}^{2} + {\beta}^{2} = 8$

questions.q: Let $f, g: \left(0, \infty\right) \to R$ be two functions defined by $f\left(x\right) = {∫}_{- x}^{x}\left(\left|t\right| - {t}^{2}\right){e}^{- {t}^{2}}dt$ and $g\left(x\right) = {∫}_{0}^{{x}^{2}}t\dfrac{1}{2}{e}^{- {t}^{2}}dt$. Then the value of $9\left(f\left(\sqrt{{\log}_{e}9} + g\left(\sqrt{{\log}_{e}9}\right\right)\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given: $g\left(x\right) = {∫}_{0}^{{x}^{2}}t\dfrac{1}{2}{e}^{- t}dt$

Let, $t = {y}^{2}$

$⇒ dt = 2ydy$

$⇒ g\left(x\right) = {∫}_{0}^{x}2{y}^{2}{e}^{- {y}^{2}}dy$

$⇒ g\left(x\right) = 2{∫}_{0}^{x}{t}^{2}{e}^{- {t}^{2}}dt$

Also, $f\left(x\right) = 2{∫}_{0}^{x}\left(t - {t}^{2}\right){e}^{- {t}^{2}}dt$y

$⇒ f\left(x\right) + g\left(x\right) = 2{∫}_{0}^{x}t{e}^{- {t}^{2}}dt$

Let, ${t}^{2} = p$

$⇒ 2tdt = dp$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) + g\left(x\right) = {∫}_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{e}^{- p}dp$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) + g\left(x\right) = 1 - {e}^{- {x}^{2}}$

$⇒ 9f\left(\sqrt{{\log}_{e}9}\right) + g\left(\sqrt{{\log}_{e}9}\right) = 9\left(1 - {e}^{- log9}\right)$

$⇒ 9f\left(\sqrt{{\log}_{e}9}\right) + g\left(\sqrt{{\log}_{e}9}\right) = 9\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{9}\right)$

$⇒ 9f\left(\sqrt{{\log}_{e}9}\right) + g\left(\sqrt{{\log}_{e}9}\right) = 8$

questions.q: $\left|\dfrac{120}{{\pi}^{3}}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{{x}^{2}sinxcosx}{\sin^{4}x + \cos^{4}x}dx\right|$ is equal to ______.
questions.solution:
Let, $I = {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{{x}^{2}sinxcosx}{\sin^{4}x + \cos^{4}x} d x$

Now using the property ${∫}_{0}^{2a}f\left(x\right) d x = {∫}_{0}^{a}f\left(x\right) d x + {∫}_{0}^{a}f\left(2a - x\right) d x$ we get,

$⇒ I = {∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{sinxcosx}{\sin^{4}x + \cos^{4}x}\left({x}^{2} - {\left(\pi - x\right)}^{2}\right) d x$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{sinxcosx}{\sin^{4}x + \cos^{4}x}\left(2\pi x - {\pi}^{2}\right) d x$

$⇒ I = 2\pi\mathop{\mathop{{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{x \cdot sinxcosx}{\sin^{4}x + \cos^{4}x} d x}_{⏟}}_{{I}_{1}} - {\pi}^{2}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{sinxcosx}{\sin^{4}x + \cos^{4}x} d x$

Now, solving ${I}_{1} = {∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{x \cdot sinxcosx}{\sin^{4}x + \cos^{4}x}dx . . . . \left(1\right)$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = {∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) \cdot sinxcosx}{\sin^{4}x + \cos^{4}x}dx . . . . \left(2\right)$

Adding both equations we get,

$⇒ 2{I}_{1} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{sinxcosx}{\sin^{4}x + \cos^{4}x}dx$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{sinxcosx}{\sin^{4}x + \cos^{4}x}dx$

Now, putting the value in $I$ we get,

$⇒ I = 2\pi \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{4}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{x \cdot sinxcosx}{\sin^{4}x + \cos^{4}x}dx - {\pi}^{2}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{sinxcosx}{\sin^{4}x + \cos^{4}x} d x$

$⇒ I = - \dfrac{{\pi}^{2}}{2}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{sinxcosx}{\sin^{4}x + \cos^{4}x} d x$

$⇒ I = - \dfrac{{\pi}^{2}}{2}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{sinxcosx}{1 - 2\sin^{2}x\cos^{2}x} d x$

$⇒ I = - \dfrac{{\pi}^{2}}{2}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}sin2x}{1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin^{2}2x} d x$

$⇒ I = - \dfrac{{\pi}^{2}}{2}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{sin2x}{2 - \sin^{2}2x} d x$

$⇒ I = - \dfrac{{\pi}^{2}}{2}{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{sin2x}{1 + \cos^{2}2x} d x$

Now, let $cos2x = t ⇒ - 2sin2xdx = dt$

$⇒ I = - \dfrac{{\pi}^{2}}{2}{∫}_{1}^{- 1}\dfrac{- \dfrac{1}{2}}{1 + {t}^{2}} d t$

$⇒ I = - \dfrac{{\pi}^{2}}{4}{∫}_{- 1}^{1}\dfrac{1}{1 + {t}^{2}} d t$

$⇒ I = - \dfrac{{\pi}^{2}}{4} \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2} = - \dfrac{{\pi}^{3}}{8}$

Hence, $\dfrac{120}{{\pi}^{3}}\left|{∫}_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{{x}^{2}sinxcosx}{\sin^{4}x + \cos^{4}x} d x\right| = \dfrac{120}{{\pi}^{3}} \times \dfrac{{\pi}^{3}}{8} = 15$

questions.q: Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function defined by $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{4}^{x}}{{4}^{x} + 2}$ and $M = \mathop{∫}_{f\left(a\right)}^{f\left(1 - a\right)}x\sin^{4}\left(x\left(1 - x\right)\right)dx$, $N = \mathop{∫}_{f\left(a\right)}^{f\left(1 - a\right)}\sin^{4}\left(x\left(1 - x\right)\right)dx; a \ne \dfrac{1}{2}$. If $\alphaM = \betaN, \alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{N}$, then the least value of ${\alpha}^{2} + {\beta}^{2}$ is equal to ______
questions.solution:
Given,

$f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{4}^{x}}{{4}^{x} + 2}$

$⇒ f\left(1 - x\right) = \dfrac{{4}^{1 - x}}{{4}^{1 - x} + 2}$

$⇒ f\left(1 - x\right) = \dfrac{4}{4 + 2 \cdot {4}^{x}} = \dfrac{2}{2 + {4}^{x}}$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) + f\left(1 - x\right) = 1$

Now, solving $M = \mathop{∫}_{f\left(a\right)}^{f\left(1 - a\right)}x \cdot \sin^{4}\left(x\left(1 - x\right)\right)dx$

Now, using the formula ${∫}_{a}^{b}f\left(x\right) d x = {∫}_{a}^{b}f\left(a + b - x\right) d x$ we get,

$⇒ M = \mathop{∫}_{f\left(a\right)}^{f\left(1 - a\right)}\left(f\left(a\right) + f\left(1 - a\right) - x\right) \cdot \sin^{4}\left(f\left(a\right) + f\left(1 - a\right) - x\right)\left(1 - \left(f\left(a\right) + f\left(1 - a\right) - x\right)\right)dx$

$⇒ M = \mathop{∫}_{f\left(a\right)}^{f\left(1 - a\right)}\left(1 - x\right) \cdot \sin^{4}\left(\left(1 - x\right)x\right)dx$

$⇒ M = \mathop{∫}_{f\left(a\right)}^{f\left(1 - a\right)}\sin^{4}\left(\left(1 - x\right)x\right)dx - \mathop{∫}_{f\left(a\right)}^{f\left(1 - a\right)}x \cdot \sin^{4}\left(\left(1 - x\right)x\right)dx$

$⇒ M = N - M$

$⇒ 2M = N$

So, on comparing we get, $\alpha = 2, \beta = 1$

Hence, ${\alpha}^{2} + {\beta}^{2} = {2}^{2} + {1}^{2} = 5$

questions.q: Let $S = \left(- 1, \infty\right)$ and $f: S \to \mathbb{R}$ be defined as $f\left(x\right) = \mathop{∫}_{- 1}^{x}{\left({e}^{t} - 1\right)}^{11}{\left(2t - 1\right)}^{5}{\left(t - 2\right)}^{7}{\left(t - 3\right)}^{12}{\left(2t - 10\right)}^{61}dt$. Let $p =$ Sum of square of the values of $x$, where $f\left(x\right)$ attains local maxima on $S$. and $q =$Sum of the values of $x$, where $f\left(x\right)$ attains local minima on $S$. Then, the value of ${p}^{2} + 2q$ is ________
questions.solution:
Given,

$f\left(x\right) = \mathop{∫}_{- 1}^{x}{\left({e}^{t} - 1\right)}^{11}{\left(2t - 1\right)}^{5}{\left(t - 2\right)}^{7}{\left(t - 3\right)}^{12}{\left(2t - 10\right)}^{61}dt$

Now, differentiating the above integral using Newton Leibnitz's theorem, we get,

${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = {\left({e}^{x} - 1\right)}^{11}{\left(2x - 1\right)}^{5}{\left(x - 2\right)}^{7}{\left(x - 3\right)}^{12}{\left(2x - 10\right)}^{61}$

Now, from the above diagram using first derivative test we get,

Local minima at $x = \dfrac{1}{2}, x = 5$

questions.q: If the integral $525\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}sin2xcos\dfrac{11}{2}x\left(1 + cos\dfrac{5}{2}x\right)\dfrac{1}{2}dx$ is equal to $\left(n\sqrt{2} - 64\right)$, then $n$ is equal to ________
questions.solution:
Let,

$I = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}sin2xcos\dfrac{11}{2}x\left(1 + cos\dfrac{5}{2}x\right)\dfrac{1}{2}dx$

Let $cosx = {t}^{2} ⇒ sinxdx = - 2tdt$

$∴ I = - 4\mathop{∫}_{1}^{0}{t}^{2} ⋅ {t}^{11}\sqrt{\left(1 + {t}^{5}\right)}\left(t\right)dt$

$⇒ I = 4\mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}{t}^{14}\sqrt{\left(1 + {t}^{5}\right)}dt$

Now, let $1 + {t}^{5} = {k}^{2}$

$⇒ 5{t}^{4}dt = 2kdk$

$∴ I = 4 ⋅ \mathop{∫}_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}{\left({k}^{2} - 1\right)}^{2} ⋅ k \cdot \dfrac{2k}{5}dk$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{8}{5}\mathop{∫}_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}{k}^{6} - 2{k}^{4} + {k}^{2}dk$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{8}{5}{\left[\dfrac{{k}^{7}}{7} - \dfrac{2{k}^{5}}{5} + \dfrac{{k}^{3}}{3}\right]}_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{8}{5}\left[\dfrac{8\sqrt{2}}{7} - \dfrac{8\sqrt{2}}{5} + \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} - \dfrac{1}{7} + \dfrac{2}{5} - \dfrac{1}{3}\right]$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{8}{5}\left[\dfrac{22\sqrt{2}}{105} - \dfrac{8}{105}\right]$

$⇒ 525 ⋅ I = 176\sqrt{2} - 64$

Hence, on comparing we get, $n = 176$

questions.q: Let $y = f ( x )$ be a thrice differentiable function in $( - 5, 5 )$. Let the tangents to the curve $y = f ( x )$ at $( 1, f ( 1 ) )$ and $( 3, f ( 3 ) )$ make angles $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, respectively with positive $x$-axis. If $27{∫}_{1}^{3}\left({\left({f}^{'}\left(t\right)\right)}^{2} + 1\right){f}^{"}\left(t\right)dt = \alpha + \beta\sqrt{3}$ where $\alpha, \beta$ are integers, then the value of $\alpha + \beta$ equals
questions.solution:
Given: 

$y = f\left(x\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = {f}^{'}\left(x\right)$

${\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}_{\left(1, f\left(1\right)\right)} = {f}^{'}\left(1\right) = tan\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(1\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} . . . \left(i\right)$

${\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}_{\left(3, f\left(3\right)\right)} = {f}^{'}\left(3\right) = tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(3\right) = 1 . . . \left(ii\right)$

It is given that, $27{∫}_{1}^{3}\left({\left({f}^{'}\left(t\right)\right)}^{2} + 1\right){f}^{"}\left(t\right)dt = \alpha + \beta\sqrt{3}$

Let, $I = {∫}_{1}^{3}\left({\left({f}^{'} ( t )\right)}^{2} + 1\right){f}^{"}\left(t\right)dt$

Putting, ${f}^{'} ( t ) = z ⇒ {f}^{"}\left(t\right)dt = dz$

$z = {f}^{'} ( 3 ) = 1$

$z = {f}^{'}\left(1\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}^{1}\left({z}^{2} + 1\right)dz$

$⇒ I = {\left(\dfrac{{z}^{3}}{3} + z\right)}_{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}^{1}$

$⇒ I = \left(\dfrac{1}{3} + 1\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{3} \cdot \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{4}{3} - \dfrac{10}{9\sqrt{3}}$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{4}{3} - \dfrac{10}{27}\sqrt{3}$

$⇒ \alpha + \beta\sqrt{3} = 27\left(\dfrac{4}{3} - \dfrac{10}{27}\sqrt{3}\right)$

$⇒ \alpha + \beta\sqrt{3} = 36 - 10\sqrt{3}$

$⇒ \alpha = 36, \beta = - 10$

$⇒ \alpha + \beta = 36 - 10$

$⇒ \alpha + \beta = 26$

questions.q: Let $f: R \to R$ be defined $f\left(x\right) = a{e}^{2x} + b{e}^{x} + cx$. If $f ( 0 ) = - 1, {f}^{'}\left({\log}_{e}2\right) = 21$ and ${∫}_{0}^{log4}\left(f\left(x\right) - cx\right)dx = \dfrac{39}{2}$, then the value of $| a + b + c |$ equals:
questions.solution:
Given: $f\left(x\right) = a{e}^{2x} + b{e}^{x} + cx, f\left(0\right) = - 1, {f}^{'}\left(log2\right) = 21, {∫}_{0}^{log4}\left(f\left(x\right) - cx\right) = \dfrac{39}{2}$

$⇒ f\left(0\right) = a + b = - 1 . . . \left(i\right)$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 2a{e}^{2x} + b{e}^{x} + c$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(log2\right) = 2a\left(4\right) + b\left(2\right) + c = 21$

$⇒ 8a + 2b + c = 21 . . . \left(ii\right)$

Also, ${∫}_{0}^{log4}\left(a{e}^{2x} + b{e}^{x} + cx - cx\right) = \dfrac{39}{2}$

$⇒ {∫}_{0}^{log4}\left(a{e}^{2x} + b{e}^{x}\right) = \dfrac{39}{2}$

$⇒ {\left[\dfrac{a{e}^{2x}}{2} + b{e}^{x}\right]}_{0}^{log4} = \dfrac{39}{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{a{e}^{2log4}}{2} + b{e}^{log4} - \dfrac{a}{2} - b = \dfrac{39}{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{15a}{2} + 3b = \dfrac{39}{2}$

$⇒ 15a + 6b = 39$

Using equation $\left(i\right)$,

$⇒ 15a + 6\left(- 1 - a\right) = 39$

$⇒ 15a - 6 - 6a = 39$

$⇒ 9a = 45$

$⇒ a = 5$

$⇒ b = - 1 - 5 = - 6$

$⇒ c = 21 - 8a - 2b$

$⇒ c = 21 - 40 + 12 = - 7$

$⇒ c = - 7$

$⇒ \left|a + b + c\right| = 8$

questions.q: The value $9{∫}_{0}^{9}\left[\sqrt{\dfrac{10x}{x + 1}}\right]dx$, where $t$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$, is _____.
questions.solution:
Let,

$I = {∫}_{0}^{9}\left[\sqrt{\dfrac{10x}{x + 1}}dx\right]$

The square of integers are $0, 1, 4, 9, . . .$

$⇒ 0 = \dfrac{10x}{x + 1} ⇒ x = 0 . . . \left(i\right)$

$⇒ 1 = \dfrac{10x}{x + 1} ⇒ x + 1 = 10x$

$⇒ x = \dfrac{1}{9} . . . \left(ii\right)$

$⇒ 4 = \dfrac{10x}{x + 1} ⇒ 4x + 4 = 10x$

$⇒ x = \dfrac{2}{3} . . . \left(iii\right)$

$⇒ 9 = \dfrac{10x}{x + 1} ⇒ 9x + 9 = 10x$

$⇒ x = 9 . . . \left(iv\right)$

Now, from the above equations using the law ${∫}_{a}^{b}f\left(x\right) d x = {∫}_{a}^{c}f\left(x\right) d x + {∫}_{c}^{d}f\left(x\right) d x + {∫}_{d}^{b}f\left(x\right) d x$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{1}{9}}\left(0\right)dx + {∫}_{\dfrac{1}{9}}^{\dfrac{2}{3}}\left(1\right)dx + {∫}_{\dfrac{2}{3}}^{9}\left(2\right)dx$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{2}{3} - \dfrac{1}{9} + 2\left(9 - \dfrac{2}{3}\right)$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{155}{9}$

$⇒ 9I = 155$

questions.q: The value of $\lim_{n \to \infty}\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{n}\dfrac{{n}^{3}}{\left({n}^{2} + {k}^{2}\right)\left({n}^{2} + 3{k}^{2}\right)}$ is :
questions.solution:
Given, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{n}\dfrac{{n}^{3}}{\left({n}^{2} + {k}^{2}\right)\left({n}^{2} + 3{k}^{2}\right)}$

$= \lim_{n \to \infty}\dfrac{1}{n}\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{\left(1 + \dfrac{{k}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}\right)\left(1 + 3 \cdot \dfrac{{k}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}\right)}$

Now, using limit as a sum integral we get,

$= {∫}_{0}^{1}\dfrac{dx}{\left(1 + {x}^{2}\right)\left(1 + 3{x}^{2}\right)}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[{∫}_{0}^{1}\dfrac{3}{\left(1 + 3{x}^{2}\right)} - \dfrac{1}{\left(1 + {x}^{2}\right)}\right]dx$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[{∫}_{0}^{1}\dfrac{1}{\left({\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)}^{2} + {x}^{2}\right)} - \dfrac{1}{\left(1 + {x}^{2}\right)}\right]dx$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}{\left[\sqrt{3}\tan^{- 1}\left(\sqrt{3}x\right) - \tan^{- 1}x\right]}_{0}^{1}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\sqrt{3}\tan^{- 1}\left(\sqrt{3}\right) - \tan^{- 1}1\right]$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\sqrt{3} \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}} - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$

$= \dfrac{13\pi}{8 \cdot ( 4\sqrt{3} + 3 )}$

questions.q: If ${∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}\sqrt{1 - sin2x}dx = \alpha + \beta\sqrt{2} + \gamma\sqrt{3}$, where $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$ are rational numbers, then $3\alpha + 4\beta - \gamma$ is equal to _____.
questions.solution:
Given,

${∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}\sqrt{1 - sin2x}dx = \alpha + \beta\sqrt{2} + \gamma\sqrt{3}$

Now, let $I = {∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}\sqrt{1 - sin2x}dx$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}} | sinx - cosx | dx$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}} ( cosx - sinx ) dx + {∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}} ( sinx - cosx ) dx$

$⇒ I = - 1 + 2\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{3}$

Now, comparing with 

$I = \alpha + \beta\sqrt{2} + \gamma\sqrt{3}$

We get, $\alpha = - 1, \beta = 2, \gamma = - 1$

Hence, $3\alpha + 4\beta - \gamma = - 3 + 8 + 1 = 6$

questions.q: For $x \in \left(- \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, if $y\left(x\right) = ∫ \dfrac{cosec x + sinx}{cosec xsecx + tanx\sin^{2}x}dx$ and $\lim_{x \to {\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)}^{-}}y\left(x\right) = 0$ then $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given:

$f\left(x\right) = ∫ \dfrac{cosecx + sinx}{cosecxsecx + tanx\sin^{2}x}dx$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = ∫ \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{sinx} + sinx}{\dfrac{1}{sinxcosx} + \dfrac{sinx}{cosx}\left(\sin^{2}x\right)}dx$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = ∫ \dfrac{\dfrac{1 + \sin^{2}x}{sinx}}{\dfrac{1 + \sin^{4}x}{sinxcosx}}dx$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = ∫ \dfrac{\left(1 + \sin^{2}x\right)cosx}{1 + \sin^{4}x}dx$

Let, $sinx = t$

$cosxdx = dt$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = ∫ \dfrac{1 + {t}^{2}}{1 + {t}^{4}}dt$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = ∫ \dfrac{1 + \dfrac{1}{{t}^{2}}}{{t}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{{t}^{2}}}dt$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = ∫ \dfrac{1 + \dfrac{1}{{t}^{2}}}{{\left(t - \dfrac{1}{t}\right)}^{2} + 2}dt$

Let, $t - \dfrac{1}{t} = u$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = ∫ \dfrac{1}{{u}^{2} + 2}du$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{u}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + C$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{t - \dfrac{1}{t}}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + C$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{sinx - \dfrac{1}{sinx}}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + C$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{sinx - cosecx}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + C$

Now, $\lim_{x \to \dfrac{\pi}{2} -}f\left(x\right) = 0$

$⇒ \lim_{x \to \dfrac{\pi}{2} -}f\left(x\right) = \lim_{x \to \dfrac{\pi}{2} -}\left[\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{sinx - cosecx}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + C\right] = 0$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan^{- 1}\left(0\right) + C = 0$

$⇒ C = 0$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{sinx - cosecx}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$

$⇒ y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{sin\dfrac{\pi}{4} - cosec\dfrac{\pi}{4}}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$

$⇒ y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$

$⇒ y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{- 1}{\sqrt{2}}}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$

$⇒ y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{- 1}{2}\right)$
